title: S7 Design Notes
text:
Preface
These are working notes on designing object systems with S7 in R and on the larger programming ideas that determine whether such systems clarify a domain or merely add ceremony. They ask one recurring question:
The answer is a style of design, not an S7 API catalog. Define what a meaningful thing is, establish the contracts that can be established at its boundary, and then build the program from those things and operations that preserve or deliberately transform their meaning. The contrast is practical: without a domain model, each consumer receives loose data and must rediscover whether a string is an identifier, whether two endpoints are ordered, whether an omitted field differs from null, and whether a failure should stop or accumulate. With a good model, those decisions have names and homes.
S7 contributes nominal classes, properties, validation, and generic dispatch, but the larger subject is how to make domain concepts, admissible states, relationships, and operations explicit. The notes therefore move repeatedly between mechanics and consequences: not only what S7 permits, but what a choice lets downstream code stop doing.
The intended outcome is practical. A reader should be able to identify concepts worth naming, place each rule at the boundary that can enforce it, choose between a reusable property and an independent class, distinguish an editable value from a A value representing a fact at a point in time, often with a public policy that forbids revision.read-only snapshot or a An object with shared identity or a live lifecycle whose aliases must observe the same evolving state.reference owner, design nouns and verbs together, and show which checks and branches disappear from downstream code. The goal is not maximum typing. It is a representation whose extra structure pays for itself in simpler consumers.

title: S7 Design Notes
text:
Evidence and register
The prose moves among four kinds of claim. A documented mechanism is behavior promised by official documentation. A version-verified mechanic has also been exercised against the stated R and package versions; it is a fact about those versions and should be rechecked after relevant upgrades. A published example is a design observed in public package source, documentation, or tests. Recurrence across independent packages strengthens the example, but neither recurrence nor popularity turns a pattern into a law. A recommendation is the editorial conclusion drawn from mechanisms, examples, and trade-offs. Imperative language states a strong default that may be overruled for a stated reason, not an exceptionless command.
This distinction matters because the chapters intentionally braid API facts, empirical observations, and design judgment. A validator running after replacement is a mechanic; choosing a class validator as the home of a particular relationship is a design decision. Readers should be able to tell which kind of claim they are being asked to trust.
The inquiry ledger records version-sensitive claims, unresolved tensions, and the evidence that would change a recommendation. Public sources are collected in the sources appendix. Examples and provenance in the published notes are limited to public source, documentation, tests, specifications, talks, and literature. Private code, local notes, and chat transcripts are not evidence here.

title: S7 Design Notes
text:
How to read
The chapters form an argument, but they can also be entered by problem. The overview states the whole position in miniature. The first three chapters establish the foundation. Object Systems explains why R’s message-passing and generic-function traditions lead to different designs and why S7 asks for a vocabulary of verbs as well as nouns. Values and State separates editable values, A value representing a fact at a point in time, often with a public policy that forbids revision.read-only snapshots, and An object with shared identity or a live lifecycle whose aliases must observe the same evolving state.reference owners, then follows the consequences into aliasing, process boundaries, MVU, and grouped replacement. Types and Meaning is the conceptual center: it connects The class, shape, cardinality, presence policy, default behavior, and intrinsic constraints attached to one property position.property contracts, A nominal class that preserves a domain concept independently so it can travel through the program or participate in dispatch.semantic classes, presence and defaults, wire representations, and the co-design of domain nouns and verbs.
The next three chapters ask where laws and variation belong. Parse, Don’t Validate places checks at the smallest boundary with enough information and explains what construction can and cannot certify. Composition and Dispatch separates unions, variant families, inheritance, interfaces, and failure protocols. Documents, Schemas, and Languages treats documents as compiler input: representations that must preserve, normalize, and sometimes defer to external authority.
The ecosystem field guide then tests these ideas against public packages. The doctrine compresses the argument into reviewable defaults, the playbooks organize common opening situations, and the middlegame compares plausible representations once real constraints begin to interact. The glossary collects the recurring design vocabulary, while the inquiry ledger keeps unsettled or version-sensitive claims visible rather than smoothing them into doctrine.
If you read only two chapters, read the overview and Types and Meaning. If you are beginning a design, use the playbooks alongside them. If you are debugging a modeling decision, begin with the chapter whose boundary is in question: lifecycle, contract placement, alternatives, or wire projection.

title: S7 Design Notes
text:
Editorial policy
These notes are deliberately opinionated, but they are also revisable. A counterexample belongs in the inquiry ledger before it silently weakens a recommendation. A pattern seen once remains an example; repeated independent public sightings can strengthen it. Version-verified mechanics remain tied to their version until rerun. New playbooks should correspond to genuinely new design situations, not merely new packages wearing familiar shapes.
Most importantly, corrections are additive when the evidence allows it. A qualification should narrow an overclaim without erasing the useful reasoning that made the claim memorable. “S7 objects are immutable,” for example, is too strong; the better account distinguishes replacement-based editable values, read-only API policy, and reference-valued payloads while retaining the local reasoning that value-oriented design buys. The same standard governs the book: preserve the mechanism, restore the argument, and state the boundary.
Corrections and counterexamples are welcome through the issue tracker.

title: 1  Overview: The Whole Argument in Miniature
text:
1.1 1. Type-driven design makes domain knowledge explicit
The central question is simple:
The answer is to define meaningful values, establish their contracts at the right boundaries, and compose operations that preserve or deliberately transform that meaning. The following ten theses summarize the argument.
Type-driven design is a way of structuring thought: identify domain concepts, admissible states, relationships, and operations, then represent them in the values and contracts from which the program is composed. The mechanism in R is runtime construction, validation, and dispatch, but the consequence is larger than catching bad values. A named DateRange can retain the fact that its endpoints are ordered; a raw pair of dates forces every consumer to infer which is first, decide whether equality is allowed, and repeat the check.
S7 provides nominal classes, properties, validators, and generic dispatch for carrying this knowledge. A useful model is therefore measured not by how many classes it creates, but by how much rediscovery it removes. See Types and Meaning.

title: 1  Overview: The Whole Argument in Miniature
text:
1.2 2. Nouns and verbs are co-designed
In S7’s generic-function tradition, classes describe domain nouns and generics describe domain verbs. Methods belong to generics rather than being stored inside classes, so behavior is organized around operations that many types may support. That mechanism changes the design process: a model is not finished when its property graph looks plausible. Asking how values will be render()ed, combine()d, prepare()d, or serialized often exposes a distinction the nouns missed; a newly distinguished noun may in turn reveal a clean dispatch axis or a law shared by several operations.
A good design therefore iterates between representative values and the operations consumers need. Nouns without verbs become inert schemas; verbs without meaningful nouns become branches over loose data. Co-design lets each side correct the other. See Object Systems.

title: 1  Overview: The Whole Argument in Miniature
text:
1.3 3. Choose the substrate by semantics
S7 is useful for domain values with invariants and dispatchable behavior. vctrs is useful for homogeneous vectors that must slice, recycle, and inhabit data-frame columns. R6 objects and environments are useful for shared identity and live resources. S3 remains effective for lightweight interoperability and for designs driven by an existing external registry. The choice determines which promises are natural: vector algebra, nominal contracts, or shared identity.
Real systems therefore combine substrates instead of choosing a camp. ellmer’s R6 Chat owns an ongoing conversation, network activity, and an accumulating lifecycle; its S7 Turn, Content, Model, and Provider objects carry inspectable records and descriptions through that process. The contrast is memorable because each system does the job its semantics fit. S7 must earn its place through meaning, invariants, operations, or composition, not merely through formality.

title: 1  Overview: The Whole Argument in Miniature
section: 1.4 4. Separate editable values, read-only snapshots, and reference owners
text:
1.4 4. Separate editable values, read-only snapshots, and reference owners
An editable S7 value changes through replacement: an operation returns a revised value while other bindings ordinarily retain the prior one. This makes branching and history explicit—a draft can become two candidate drafts without either candidate silently changing the other. A read-only snapshot is also a value, but its public API intentionally offers no revision path because it records a completed fact. A reference owner has shared identity, a live resource, or an observable lifecycle, so aliases are expected to observe the same change.
These are three lifecycle policies, not synonyms for mutable and immutable. A draft document may be an editable value, its published form a snapshot, and the editor coordinating both a reference owner. Copy-on-modify does not make every S7 property read-only, and wrapping an environment, R6 object, or external pointer does not turn the payload into a value. See Values and State.

title: 1  Overview: The Whole Argument in Miniature
section: 1.5 5. Put each contract at the smallest boundary that can state it
text:
1.5 5. Put each contract at the smallest boundary that can state it
Property definitions carry intrinsic shape, cardinality, membership, bounds, and local presence policy. Class validators carry relationships among one object’s properties. Aggregate roots carry rules over contained objects and references. Contextual operations carry checks that require datasets, metadata, resources, or authority. The mechanism follows information visibility: a scalar property can know that alpha lies in [0, 1], but only a style aggregate can know that every layer names an existing source, and only an operation with runtime metadata can know that the source still exists.
Placing each rule once lets higher layers trust lower ones and keeps one predicate from drifting across constructors, methods, and serializers. Construction certifies only the invariants visible at that boundary and preserved by supported transformations; it is a bounded certificate, not a claim of omniscience.

title: 1  Overview: The Whole Argument in Miniature
text:
1.6 6. Construction should retain knowledge
A useful boundary does more than reject bad input. Rejection says only “not this”; retention lets later code rely on what was established. A DateRange records ordered endpoints, explicit candidate values record tuning intent that would otherwise be guessed from vector shape, and a prepared run can record completion of data-dependent checks. The consequence is fewer repeated questions: possession of the richer value answers them.
This is the dynamic-language form of parse, don’t validate, with an important qualification. Strict construction of known values can coexist with tolerant parsing when uncertainty is represented explicitly as an unknown or partial variant with diagnostics. Retaining uncertainty is still retaining knowledge; silently collapsing it to a familiar value is not.

title: 1  Overview: The Whole Argument in Miniature
section: 1.7 7. Alternatives, families, and failure protocols are separate designs
text:
1.7 7. Alternatives, families, and failure protocols are separate designs
An S7 union states which alternatives a property accepts, and those alternatives may include primitive or domain classes. Concrete classes preserve variant identity. An abstract parent supplies shared schema or a dispatch protocol, but does not seal the family. These mechanisms solve different problems: acceptance, identity, shared behavior, and extension. Coverage tests and loud fallbacks help detect unsupported cases; neither proves exhaustiveness.
Failure adds a second axis that is easy to hide. A Success/Failure outcome family represents what happened, but it does not decide what happens when several outcomes are combined. One workflow may stop on the first failure, another may accumulate all diagnostics, and an interactive boundary may turn the same failure into an R condition. Modeling the failure shape and the composition protocol separately prevents a sum type from smuggling in one global control-flow policy.

title: 1  Overview: The Whole Argument in Miniature
section: 1.8 8. One meaning may have several deliberate projections
text:
1.8 8. One meaning may have several deliberate projections
An authoritative declaration can drive a native validator, schema, documentation, UI description, or serializer. The mechanism is projection: one owned semantic specification is interpreted into several artifacts. The consequence is not infallibility but a smaller agreement problem. Instead of maintaining five independent definitions, tests can check that each generator faithfully projects the one source.
This makes generation from an owned semantic specification a legitimate architecture. Blindly generating a class graph from incidental foreign structure is different: it imports someone else’s arrangement without first deciding which distinctions have meaning in the R API.

title: 1  Overview: The Whole Argument in Miniature
section: 1.9 9. Documents require explicit preservation and authority policies
text:
1.9 9. Documents require explicit preservation and authority policies
A document is often a declarative program: a style, query, configuration, or conversation transcript is data that another engine will interpret. The R package is therefore closer to a compiler front-end than a bag of setters. Its object graph should make meaningful constructions convenient, preserve the distinctions required for a faithful projection, and delegate full conformance when an external engine is the authority.
A parser, adapter, compiler, or serializer should consequently say what it preserves, normalizes, loses, and compares. External authority may act as a wire-format gate, a runtime metadata provider, or a test oracle. Typing depth is chosen per node: semantic nodes with identity or operations deserve types, extensible key spaces may remain validated bags, and embedded languages can remain opaque until consumers need to inspect them. A schema is an important compiler input and contract, not automatically the ideal native class graph.

title: 1  Overview: The Whole Argument in Miniature
section: 1.10 10. General machinery must earn its keep; meaningful concepts need not
text:
1.10 10. General machinery must earn its keep; meaningful concepts need not
Every abstraction introduces a new place to look. It earns that indirection when it absorbs a real axis of change: generic-to-method dispatch absorbs behavioral variation across types, a semantic class prevents meanings with the same primitive representation from being confused, and a wire-name map contains serialization churn. A pass-through wrapper or speculative factory with one use merely moves code without removing a decision.
The rule of three is therefore a useful restraint on generalized factories, metamodels, and framework layers. It is not a requirement to leave an important domain concept unnamed until it appears three times. Start from the domain and intended consumers, sketch representative values and operations, record the contracts encountered, and extract reusable machinery only from real repetition. A large flat class or generated facade is not wrong merely because it has many fields; the question is whether its shape is authoritative and whether it makes its consumers simpler. Abstractions pay rent by deleting rediscovery, branching, duplication, or coordinated change.

The remaining chapters develop these theses through mechanics, public package examples, decision guides, and executable laws. The Doctrine compresses them for design reviews.

title: 2  Object Systems: What Kind of OOP S7 Is
text:
2.1 Two traditions of object orientation
Object-oriented programming is not one idea but at least two, and R is unusual in making both traditions ordinary parts of package design. The distinction matters because it changes what the design must name, where extension lives, and which intuitions transfer safely from other languages.
The message-passing tradition descends from Smalltalk through C++, Java, Python, and JavaScript. Objects encapsulate state and behavior together; you send a message to an object (obj.method(arg)) and the object decides how to respond. The class is the unit of organization: it owns its methods, controls access to its fields, and behavior extension means subclassing or mixins. In R this tradition is represented by R6 (and the older Reference Classes), where objects are environments with attached functions and genuine mutable state.
The generic-function tradition descends from CLOS (the Common Lisp Object System) through Dylan and Julia. Here classes define data and identity while behavior lives in generic functions — ordinary-looking functions that select an implementation (a method) based on the classes of their arguments. A method call looks like any function call: speak(dog), not dog.speak(). S3, S4, and S7 are all in this family; the S7 documentation calls it “functional OOP.” From the outside, behavior remains function application and composes naturally with R’s functional style: values flow through ordinary calls and pipes, methods remain implementations of verbs rather than hidden entries in an object’s method table, and packages can add behavior without owning the class definition.
The philosophical difference matters for design. In message-passing OOP, the central design question is “what objects exist and what do they encapsulate?” In generic-function OOP it splits in two: “what is each thing?” (classes, properties, invariants) and “what can be done, and to which things?” (generics and their methods). A well-designed S7 system co-designs its nouns and verbs. A deliberately curated verb vocabulary — its generics — matters as much as the class graph. This is the important correction to class-centered habits: drawing a complete inheritance tree and only then asking what users need to do designs half an interface.
Consider a family of document nodes. A class-first design may distinguish nodes only by stored fields. Asking for render(), references(), and rewrite() methods can reveal that two structurally similar nodes obey different laws, while two structurally different nodes participate in the same protocol. Operations reveal distinctions the representation is missing; representations reveal useful dispatch axes and behavioral laws. The process therefore iterates: classes do not need to be finished before methods inform them, and a generic should name a stable domain action rather than expose the current storage layout.
The two traditions also produce different extension stories. In message-passing OOP, adding behavior normally means changing a class or a subclass under its control. In generic-function OOP, another package can define a new generic for existing classes or a new method for an existing generic and a new class. That openness is powerful, but it makes generic names, dispatch arguments, fallback behavior, and method laws part of the public architecture.

title: 2  Object Systems: What Kind of OOP S7 Is
section: 2.2 The landscape of R object systems
text:
2.2 The landscape of R object systems
Choosing among R’s systems is therefore not a syntax preference. The useful distinctions are representation contract, operation model, and lifecycle. A vector that must recycle correctly, a value whose construction establishes invariants, and a session whose aliases must observe the same changes have different semantics even if each could be forced into a class-shaped API.
S3 is the lingua franca: an object is any value with a class attribute, and UseMethod() dispatches on it. There are no formal fields, no validation, no guarantees — only conventions. Its virtues are near-zero ceremony and universal ecosystem reach (every print, format, summary in existence). Its vice is that nothing stops anyone from constructing garbage. S3 remains the right choice for lightweight interoperability wrappers, and it is the substrate that vctrs disciplines.
S4 provides explicit class definitions, typed slots, validity methods, and multiple dispatch. It remains important in Bioconductor and other established ecosystems. S7 pursues many of the same goals with a more regular interface and explicit interoperability with existing systems.
R6 provides message-passing OOP with reference semantics: objects are mutable, methods are attached, $clone() exists because copies are no longer automatic. R6 is not a competitor to S7; it answers a different question (identity and mutation) and appears alongside S7 in well-designed packages.
Environments are the raw material of reference semantics — mutable bags with identity — useful for caches and registries when R6’s structure would be overhead.
vctrs is not an object system so much as a rigorous S3 framework for vector types: it supplies the algebra of sizes, prototypes, casting, and coercion that makes a custom vector behave correctly in c(), [, data.frame columns, and joins. If the thing you are modeling is fundamentally a column of homogeneous values, vctrs is the answer and S7 is not; re-implementing coercion rules in S7 validators is wasted, buggy effort.
S7, finally: formal classes with typed, validated, defaulted properties; class validators for whole-object invariants; single and multiple dispatch via generics; explicit S7::super(); declared compatibility with S3 and S4 in both directions.

title: 2  Object Systems: What Kind of OOP S7 Is
section: 2.3 What is distinctive about S7 itself
text:
2.3 What is distinctive about S7 itself
Several S7 design decisions reward close attention because they enable patterns that S3/S4 made awkward.
Classes are first-class values. S7::new_class() returns an object that is simultaneously the class definition and its constructor. You call it to make instances; you pass it around like any value; you store it in lists; you write functions that return classes. This makes class factories and registries possible in ordinary R. They are useful when generated from an owned, coherent specification or demonstrated repetition; first-class classes do not by themselves justify generating a native class for every piece of foreign structure.
A practical use is a parser registry whose wire tags select constructors:
node_classes <- list(
  query = QueryNode,
  relation = RelationNode
)

construct_node <- function(input) {
  constructor <- node_classes[[input$type]]
  if (is.null(constructor)) {
    cli::cli_abort("Unknown node type {.val {input$type}}.")
  }
  do.call(constructor, input$fields)
}
The registry is data, so packages can inspect, extend, or test it without encoding the same choice in a switch() at every boundary. This is most useful when the tags and constructors belong to one coherent model; it is not a reason to manufacture classes for distinctions the domain does not use.
The same fact supports useful reflection in ordinary R code. A tool can walk class and generic metadata to report declared properties, parents, defaults, validators, methods, and dispatch information. The datarr/reflect package does exactly this — descriptor objects for properties, methods, and callables, with method tables enumerated per generic and S7’s own S7::method_explain() attached as a dispatch trace. The boundary is important: an arbitrary validator is executable code, not automatically inspectable constraint data. Documentation, schemas, and forms can be projected only from metadata and constraints the model represents explicitly. Those projections still require tests for agreement.
Properties have a full lifecycle. A property is not just a typed slot. It carries a class (which may be a union), a default (which may be a quoted expression evaluated at construction — the standard trick for required properties is default = quote(stop("Required"))), an optional validator, and optional getter/setter for computed or guarded access. This is the layer where most fine-grained design happens, and it is examined throughout Types and Meaning and Parse, Don’t Validate.
Validation is built into the object lifecycle. Class validation runs at construction and after supported property replacement, and a validator may return a character vector describing several problems. The resulting certificate is bounded by what the validator can see and by mutation paths: reference-valued payloads can change behind the wrapper without triggering outer validation. The consequences are developed in Parse, Don’t Validate.
Dispatch is explicit and disciplined. Generics declare their dispatch arguments; method signatures are checked for compatibility against the generic (a method missing an argument the generic promises produces a warning; a method without ... refuses misspelled arguments instead of silently swallowing them, a real S3 footgun). S7::super(x, to = Parent) replaces the implicit NextMethod() with an explicit statement of which parent behavior you want. Multiple dispatch exists (S7::new_generic(dispatch_args = c("x", "y"))) and, while rare, is decisive where behavior genuinely depends on two types at once — serializing a value for a dialect, converting from one type to another, combining two objects. The special classes class_any and class_missing round out multiple dispatch by matching anything and matching an absent argument respectively.
Compatibility is bidirectional. S7 methods can be registered on S3 generics; S3 and S4 classes can serve as property types (an S4 class via methods::getClass(), an S3 class via S7::new_S3_class()); S7 classes can have methods on S4 generics. This matters strategically: adopting S7 does not fence you off from the ecosystem, and hybrid designs (an S7 property holding a DBI S4 connection, an S7 class fronted by an S3 facade) are supported rather than hacked.

title: 2  Object Systems: What Kind of OOP S7 Is
section: 2.4 Choosing the substrate: a semantic decision procedure
text:
2.4 Choosing the substrate: a semantic decision procedure
The question “S7 or something else?” is answered by the semantics of the thing being modeled. The following inventory is deliberately ordered: lifecycle and vector behavior are harder to bolt on after the fact than a prettier print method.

Is it fundamentally a vector — a column of homogeneous values that must slice, concatenate, recycle, and live in data frames? Then vctrs, possibly held by an S7 object but not replaced by one.
Does it have identity and a lifetime — a conversation, a connection, a cache, an accumulating log — where two references to it must observe each other’s changes? Then reference semantics: R6 or an environment. An S7 value may snapshot it, but the live thing is a reference.
Is it a domain value — a fact, configuration, document, message, or measurement — with nominal meaning, internal laws, or behavior worth dispatching on? Then S7 is a strong candidate. If an external metadata registry already owns the contract and no additional semantic identity is needed, an S3 value plus metadata may remain the better design.
Is it a veneer over something that already works, needed only so a print method looks right? Then S3, and stop there.

The procedure is not a tournament with one winner. The most instructive designs use several systems at once, on purpose. In ellmer, the Chat object is R6 because a conversation is an ongoing process with identity — you append turns to it — while each Turn inside it is an S7 value representing a record. Whether that value is editable or exposed as a read-only snapshot is a separate API policy. In ragnar, MarkdownDocumentChunks is an S7 class that inherits from tibble: the data is fundamentally tabular (so it should behave as a data frame) but carries a @document property and domain identity on top. These are not compromises; they are the point. The systems are tools with distinct semantics, and fluency means combining them without ideology.

title: 2  Object Systems: What Kind of OOP S7 Is
text:
2.5 The expression problem, briefly
Generic-function OOP has a distinctive relationship to what Philip Wadler named the expression problem (Wadler 1998): the difficulty of adding both new data variants and new operations to a system without modifying existing code. The problem explains why verb-centered extension is more than a calling style. Class-owned methods make new variants easy (subclass) and new operations hard (edit every class). Pattern-matching functional code makes new operations easy (new function) and new variants hard (edit every match). Generic functions make both directions open: anyone can add a class and register methods for existing generics; anyone can add a generic and register methods for existing classes. ellmer exploits exactly this: adding a new LLM provider means adding a Provider subclass and registering methods on the existing generic vocabulary — no core changes.
The design opportunity is two-dimensional. A provider package can add a new Provider variant to verbs ellmer already defines; an analysis package can add a new operation over provider classes it does not own. Neither extension requires turning the class into a God object or editing a central switch. This is why an S7 API should expose a small, meaningful generic vocabulary: those verbs are the joints at which independent packages can extend the system.
The price of this openness is the absence of exhaustiveness checking: nothing verifies at definition time that every variant handles every generic. An abstract parent is not sealed, and a fallback method is not proof of coverage. Loud fallbacks plus tests that enumerate the known registry detect unsupported cases without claiming that the family is closed. These techniques are discussed in Composition and Dispatch.




Wadler, Philip. 1998. “The Expression Problem.” https://homepages.inf.ed.ac.uk/wadler/papers/expression/expression.txt.

title: 3  Values and State: Editing, Snapshots, and Reference Owners
text:
3.1 R’s physics: copy-on-modify
R usually presents a value-oriented interface. What looks like mutation — x[1] <- 5, df$col <- z, style@zoom <- 10 — is replacement followed by rebinding. The @<- form is replacement syntax as well. R may reuse or copy memory internally, and those implementation details are not a public promise of structural sharing.
For ordinary value-like payloads, revising an S7 object through replacement produces a new value for the receiving binding; another binding ordinarily continues to denote the prior value. This is editable value semantics, not field immutability. A package can additionally expose a value as a read-only snapshot by withholding public update operations, but that is an API policy rather than a consequence of S7.
Validation hooks into supported replacement paths. S7 runs validation after property replacement, so exported transformation functions can preserve the class contract. The guarantee is bounded: a validator certifies only rules it can see, and mutation inside a reference-valued property does not invoke the outer object’s validator. This is the mechanical foundation for the parse-don’t-validate discipline in Parse, Don’t Validate.

title: 3  Values and State: Editing, Snapshots, and Reference Owners
section: 3.2 Why value semantics are a superpower for domain modeling
text:
3.2 Why value semantics are a superpower for domain modeling
Rich Hickey’s “value of values” argument is useful beyond its Clojure origins (Hickey 2012). A representation whose observable domain content changes only through replacement supports local reasoning. For domain modeling, values buy:

Focused testing. Value-in, value-out functions support assertions about domain equality and serialized form without hidden lifecycle setup.
Explicit history. Keeping an earlier binding preserves a prior logical version. Storage cost depends on R’s implementation and payload; history is not universally free.
Branching. Two candidate variants of a configuration are two values. Nothing needs cloning ceremonies; ellmer’s R6 Chat needs an explicit $clone() to fork a conversation precisely because it opted out of value semantics.
Compositional reasoning. Transformations compose as functions. A pipeline style |> add_layer(l) |> set_zoom(10) makes each revision explicit.

The temptation to resist is making domain objects mutable “because updating is annoying.” The annoyance is real (deep updates in value-land involve rebuilding paths through the structure) but it is the cost side of every guarantee listed above, and R’s replacement-function machinery plus well-designed mutator generics (add_layer(style, layer) returning a new style) absorbs most of it.

title: 3  Values and State: Editing, Snapshots, and Reference Owners
text:
3.3 Three lifecycle policies
The easiest way to see the lifecycle choices is to follow one concept through time. Imagine a style being assembled in an editor. While it is a draft, adding a layer or changing a zoom range is lawful, but each operation can return a revised value. The caller can keep the prior draft, compare two candidates, or abandon one branch without coordinating aliases. This is an editable value: editable because the API supplies transformations, a value because those transformations use replacement rather than shared mutation.
When the style is published, the package may expose it as a read-only snapshot. Nothing about R’s copy mechanics has changed. The difference is policy: a completed fact has no public revision operation. If correction is needed, the program can create a new draft from the snapshot and eventually publish another snapshot, preserving which fact was current at each point.
The editor that coordinates drafts and publication is different again. It may own a live connection, autosave timer, undo cursor, and subscriptions that must all refer to the same ongoing session. That object is a reference owner. Its aliases are expected to observe the same evolving lifecycle, so an environment or R6 object expresses the concept more honestly than repeated value replacement.
The progression—draft to snapshot under the control of an owner—shows why “mutable or immutable?” is too blunt. Ask instead: what changes are lawful, who owns them, should an earlier fact remain available, and must other observers see a change immediately? Configuration, documents under construction, and query descriptions often begin as editable values; completed turns, measurements, and published documents often become snapshots; sessions, connections, and editors are reference owners.

title: 3  Values and State: Editing, Snapshots, and Reference Owners
text:
3.4 Where reference semantics genuinely belong
Value semantics are the wrong answer for a specific, identifiable class of things: those with identity and a lifetime — where the whole point is that observers share the same evolving thing.

A conversation being appended to, turn by turn.
A connection or session with a server, a file handle, a browser tab.
A cache or memoization table, whose entire purpose is coordinated mutation.
A registry that accumulates plugins or handlers at load time.
UI state observed by a reactive framework.

R expresses these with environments, R6, or external pointers. The design failure mode is not using reference semantics — it is using them where shared identity is not part of the concept. A completed turn, measurement, or published style can be a read-only snapshot. A draft style can be an editable value. The conversation or editor coordinating those values may be a reference owner.
One qualification deserves stating as a law of its own, because it bounds every claim above: value semantics is only as deep as the payload. An S7 object behaves dependably as a value only when everything reachable through its properties is itself value-like. A property holding an environment, an R6 object, an external pointer, or a connection is a reference inside a value: copying the object copies the pointer, not the contents, and every “copy” observes mutations of the shared payload. This is directly demonstrable — assign into an environment held as a property through one binding, and the change is visible through the other binding, even after the two objects have otherwise diverged. The wrapper does not immunize its contents, and changing the shared payload does not re-run the wrapper’s validator. If a class must hold a reference, document the aliasing and lifecycle contract, define whether the reference participates in domain equality or serialization, or snapshot the referenced state into plain data at the boundary.

title: 3  Values and State: Editing, Snapshots, and Reference Owners
text:
3.5 Process boundaries are serialization boundaries
Parallel workers do not turn reference-valued properties into shared state (Bengtsson 2026a, 2026b). PSOCK and future-style workers receive serialized copies of exported values; an environment copied to another process is a different environment, while a connection or external pointer may not be usable there at all. Forked workers inherit another set of hazards around live connections and foreign resources.
Pass portable S7 values across process boundaries when their payload is serializable, ensure the defining package and method registrations are available on the worker, and reconstruct live resources inside the worker from declarative specifications. During development, reference scanning such as options(future.globals.onReference = "error") can expose accidental external pointers. The architecture is the same as at a service boundary: send meaning as data; bind capabilities and resources where they will run.

title: 3  Values and State: Editing, Snapshots, and Reference Owners
text:
3.6 Functional core, imperative shell
Gary Bernhardt’s “Boundaries” talk (Bernhardt 2012) gave the canonical name to the architecture these observations imply: a functional core of pure functions over values, wrapped in a thin imperative shell that talks to the world. The shell fetches, reads, writes, streams, and mutates session state; the core decides, transforms, constructs, and validates. Values cross the boundary; decisions concentrate in the core where they are trivially testable; side effects concentrate in the shell where they are at least localized.
In R terms:

Core: S7 constructors and validators; pure transformations from object to object; serialization to and from plain lists; generation of documents, queries, expressions.
Shell: httr2 requests, file I/O, database and GDAL calls, Shiny reactivity, LLM streaming, R6 orchestrators.

ellmer is the cleanest published illustration. The R6 Chat object is the shell: it owns the HTTP lifecycle, the streaming, the tool-invocation loop, and the accumulating list of turns — a state machine with identity. Everything that flows through it is S7 values: Turn objects containing Content objects, a Model configuration, a Provider description. The values are what you inspect, test, serialize, and reprocess; the R6 object is how the process is driven. Neither system is asked to do the other’s job.
The architecture has a fully formalized variant worth knowing by name: the Model–View–Update (Elm) architecture, which the tooey terminal-UI framework brings to R. An application is organized around three callbacks: init() creates its initial state, update(model, msg) maps the current state and an incoming message to new state plus commands, and view(model, buf) renders state into a screen buffer. The framework runtime owns the terminal, clock, and keyboard input, delivers them as plain-data messages, and executes returned commands.
That architecture encourages a functional core, but ordinary R callbacks can still read global state or perform I/O; the framework cannot enforce purity. Purity is therefore an application discipline: keep effects in declared commands and runtime adapters so init(), update(), and view() remain deterministic and independently testable. Beyond UI, MVU answers a question value-oriented designs eventually face — where do events go? Events are values too: represent them explicitly and fold them into state through the update operation.
The test for whether you have the boundary right: could you reconstruct the entire domain state from the values alone, replaying or discarding the shell? If domain knowledge exists only as mutable state inside a reference object, the boundary has leaked.

title: 3  Values and State: Editing, Snapshots, and Reference Owners
text:
3.7 A taxonomy of state
“State” is not one thing. Separating its kinds prevents both over-engineering (R6 everywhere) and under-engineering (globals in disguise).
Document state — the current value of the domain object itself. Lives in S7 values; changes by replacement through constructors and mutator generics.
Derived state — anything computable from document state: an index from layer id to layer, a count, a rendered preview. The default is to not store it: compute on read, possibly via a getter-backed dynamic property. If computation is expensive, memoize outside the object (an environment keyed by a canonical domain representation). A cache inside the object introduces reference semantics and must be reflected in its aliasing, equality, and serialization contracts.
Collection state — registries of named things inside a document (sources by id, items by key). These are just properties (named lists) of an aggregate object; their invariants (unique ids, valid references) belong to that aggregate’s validator, as developed in Parse, Don’t Validate.
Session state — the live process: connections, conversations, event loops. R6 or environments, in the shell.
Configuration state — options, environment variables, credentials. Read at the boundary and passed in as values; a core function that consults options() mid-computation has smuggled in a hidden input.

title: 3  Values and State: Editing, Snapshots, and Reference Owners
text:
3.8 Grouped replacements preserve relationships
S7 validates after each property replacement. When an invariant spans several properties, sequential single-property updates can pass through transiently invalid intermediate states — and the validator will correctly reject the intermediate, even though the final state would have been fine. Suppose a class requires start <= end and both must move forward. This looks like an ordinary pair of edits:
x@start <- 15
x@end <- 20
If x currently spans 1 to 3, the first line proposes the interval 15 to 3. The class validator cannot know that another statement is coming; it sees a complete proposed object that violates start <= end, so it rejects the replacement. Reversing the statements happens to work for this direction of movement, but fails symmetrically when both endpoints move backward. The problem is not statement order. Two values that must change together are being presented as two independent transitions.
The operation should instead construct one proposed state and validate the relationship once. S7::set_props() does that. The following executable example also keeps an alias to make the value behavior visible:

Interval <- S7::new_class(
  "Interval",
  properties = list(
    start = S7::class_double,
    end = S7::class_double
  ),
  validator = function(self) {
    if (self@start > self@end) {
      "@start must not exceed @end"
    }
  }
)

original <- Interval(start = 1, end = 3)
alias <- original
revised <- S7::set_props(original, start = 15, end = 20)

data.frame(
  binding = c("alias", "revised"),
  start = c(alias@start, revised@start),
  end = c(alias@end, revised@end)
)

  binding start end
1   alias     1   3
2 revised    15  20


The result demonstrates two independent facts. alias still records the original interval, because revising the receiving binding did not mutate every alias. revised contains the jointly updated endpoints, because validation saw 15 and 20 together. The operation is transaction-like: related replacements are checked as one proposed value rather than exposed as invalid intermediate values.
The design rule that follows is: any invariant spanning multiple properties implies that every supported code path updating those properties should use one grouped replacement—usually wrapped in a domain transformation such as move_interval(x, start, end). The wrapper names the transition and prevents callers from having to remember which fields form a validation unit.
S7 also provides S7::valid_eventually() for a transformation that must perform several ordinary replacements before the object becomes valid again. It suppresses intermediate validation and validates the returned object once at the end. Prefer S7::set_props() when the change is only a grouped assignment; valid_eventually() is for a genuinely multi-step transformation. Its lower-level companion, S7::valid_implicitly(), skips even the final validation. That transfers the entire proof obligation to the caller and belongs only in measured, performance-critical internals whose validity argument is explicit and tested.

title: 3  Values and State: Editing, Snapshots, and Reference Owners
section: 3.9 Getters, setters, and the discipline of cheap access
text:
3.9 Getters, setters, and the discipline of cheap access
S7 properties may carry a getter (making the property computed and, without a setter, read-only — and excluded from the default constructor, since it is not stored state) and a setter (which receives self and value and returns the modified self, enabling normalization on write).
Two contracts deserve emphasis because S7 does not enforce them for you. First, a getter’s return value is not validated against the declared class; you are on your honor. Second, and more important as a design matter: property access must be cheap and pure. The entire mental model of an S7 object is “structured data.” A getter that performs I/O, network calls, or expensive computation silently converts data access into action-at-a-distance and destroys the reader’s ability to reason about cost or effects. Computed properties are for derivations (a duration from start and end, a full name from parts, a constant discriminator), not for laziness tricks.
Setters, symmetrically, are for normalization that preserves meaning — trimming whitespace, sorting a tag set, upgrading a bare scalar to a length-one vector. The moment a setter starts making semantic decisions or enforcing cross-property rules, it is doing a constructor’s or validator’s job in a place readers will not look.

title: 3  Values and State: Editing, Snapshots, and Reference Owners
text:
3.10 Identity, equality, and testing
Equality is a domain decision, not a synonym for identical().

Domain equality asks whether two values mean the same thing.
Canonical equality asks whether their normalized representations agree.
identical() asks whether two R objects have the same exact representation, including types and relevant attributes.
Reference identity asks whether two handles designate the same live owner.

These relations can disagree: 8 and 8L may be domain-equal but are not identical(), and two independently created values may render the same document despite incidental representational differences. Tests should name the relation they intend. Value transformations favor input/output laws and canonical projections; reference owners additionally need lifecycle and alias-observation tests.

title: 4  Types and Meaning: Semantic Types, Structure, and Type-Driven Design
text:
4.1 Three lenses on what a type is
Before designing with types it helps to hold three complementary definitions in mind.
A type is a set of values. integer between 0 and 255 names a set; nonempty string names a set. Under this lens, subtyping is subset-hood, a union type is a set union, and a validator is a membership predicate.
A type is a contract on operations. Knowing x is a Color tells you what you may do: read channels, convert to hex, blend. Under this lens, interfaces and generics define types as much as data layouts do — a “thing that can be serialized” is a type in the behavioral sense even if no class hierarchy says so.
A type is a name for meaning. EmailAddress and CustomerId may both be strings-as-sets, and support the same operations-as-contracts, yet naming them separately encodes knowledge: these are different kinds of thing, and substituting one for the other is a bug even when no operation would fail.
Static languages let a compiler exploit all three lenses. R distributes the work across constructors, property and class validation, generic dispatch, schemas, boundary checks, and tests. These mechanisms enforce different things, but they share a design move: make meaning explicit enough that consumers can rely on it.

title: 4  Types and Meaning: Semantic Types, Structure, and Type-Driven Design
section: 4.2 Structural versus nominal — and where semantics enters
text:
4.2 Structural versus nominal — and where semantics enters
Type systems differ in what makes two types “the same,” and most languages mix several mechanisms. TypeScript object types and Go interfaces are prominent structural examples: compatibility can follow from the required shape without an explicit declaration. Java class identity and Haskell newtype declarations are prominent nominal examples: distinct declarations remain distinct despite similar representations. Those languages also contain exceptions and additional mechanisms, so the contrast is a design lens rather than a complete taxonomy.
R code can be written in a structurally permissive style: a function that reaches into x$field may work on anything exposing that component. That does not make S7 structurally typed. S7 dispatch and property-class checks use declared class identity and inheritance. Shape requirements such as scalar length, names, or required components are additional runtime contracts, usually expressed by properties and validators rather than inferred from structure. An S7 design can therefore combine nominal identity with explicit shape constraints without confusing the two.
The third notion — semantic typing — is the design payoff of nominal identity. The classic statically typed device is the newtype: wrap a primitive in a distinct type (CustomerId wrapping string) so that the compiler stops you from passing a customer id where an order id is expected. The wrapper adds no structure; it adds meaning and prevents an entire class of “stringly typed” defects where everything is a character vector and nothing stops the wrong one from arriving.

title: 4  Types and Meaning: Semantic Types, Structure, and Type-Driven Design
text:
4.3 Semantic contracts and loose coupling
There is a systems-integration corollary that elevates semantic types from a convenience to an architectural principle. When two systems integrate by sharing structure — an agreed record layout — every structural change in one forces coordination with the other; the coupling is total. When they integrate by sharing semantics — agreed atomic meanings like CustomerId, EmailAddress, FloodZoneClass — each system arranges those atoms in whatever local structure suits it, and a mapping layer mediates. Structures then evolve independently while data remains meaningfully exchangeable, because the meanings are the stable contract.
(This idea is developed explicitly in data-integration languages like Taxi, where type CustomerId inherits String declarations are shared across systems precisely so models do not have to be.)
The general lesson for a multi-dialect domain is to seek stable shared meanings without assuming they are known in advance. Sketch representative documents and operations for more than one dialect, then extract the semantic concepts that survive the comparison. Modeling one dialect as universal couples every other dialect to its incidental structure; designing an “uber-schema” before seeing real consumers is the opposite error.

title: 4  Types and Meaning: Semantic Types, Structure, and Type-Driven Design
section: 4.4 A running concept: color in a style document
text:
4.4 A running concept: color in a style document
To keep the rest of the chapter concrete, consider a Color used by a style document. At first it appears to be “four numbers”: red, green, and blue channels in [0, 255], plus alpha in [0, 1]. That description already hides several decisions. Are channels integers or merely integerish numerics? Is alpha stored when omitted, and who chooses its default? Can a color travel independently of the style? Must callers blend colors, render them as hex, or preserve the exact spelling read from a wire document?
Those questions are not implementation trivia. They determine whether color is a repeated property recipe, a nominal value, or an incidental wire shape; which rules are local and which relate several channels; and whether serialization is a projection of the domain value or the source of truth for it. The sections that follow revisit the same concept as each design layer comes into view.

title: 4  Types and Meaning: Semantic Types, Structure, and Type-Driven Design
section: 4.5 A practical property and contract inventory
text:
4.5 A practical property and contract inventory
Before choosing a class graph, inventory the questions each concept raises. This is a design worksheet, not a requirement to build a property framework first. For the running color, it turns “four numbers” into the actual decisions a representation must retain:

Representation: What R class and shape are canonical? Is the value a scalar, vector, record, alternative, or collection? A color could be a length-four numeric vector or a record with named channels; the choice affects readability and projection.
Cardinality: What lengths are lawful? Are names, order, or uniqueness significant? An unnamed vector makes channel order load-bearing, while named properties make the association explicit.
Membership and bounds: Is the value drawn from an enum, literal set, interval, pattern, or other locally decidable set? Each RGB channel has a local integer and range law; alpha has a different range.
Presence: Must the resulting object contain it? Must the caller supply it? May the stored value be NULL or NA? Are zero-length and empty values meaningful? A style may require a color while allowing callers to omit alpha.
Default ownership: Does omission mean an R-owned domain default, a value supplied by an external authority, or a caller request to materialize a default later? If opaque is the domain default, R can store alpha = 1; if an external renderer chooses opacity, materializing 1 would invent knowledge the model does not own.
Relationships: Which rules mention several properties of one object, several contained objects, or external context?
Lifecycle: Is this an editable value, a read-only snapshot, or part of a reference owner?
Operations: Which verbs consume or produce it, what do they preserve, and how do they fail? blend(), as_hex(), and contrast calculations may justify color as an independent dispatchable concept.
Projection: How does it serialize, and which distinctions among omission, null, unknown, and empty must survive? A wire format may accept a hex string, an array, or an object even if the domain stores one canonical form.

The inventory determines rule placement. Intrinsic shape, cardinality, membership, bounds, and local presence policy belong in property contracts. Relationships among one object’s properties belong in its class validator. Cross-object references belong at an aggregate boundary. Rules needing data, metadata, resources, or authority belong in a named contextual operation. When one slot accepts alternatives, an S7 union may name primitive classes, domain classes, or both; a union describes accepted values, not a closed variant family. For Color, channel bounds are property contracts, the relationship among channels belongs to the Color class if one exists, and whether a foreground color meets an accessibility threshold is contextual to its background and belongs in an operation with both values.

title: 4  Types and Meaning: Semantic Types, Structure, and Type-Driven Design
section: 4.7 Type-driven design in a dynamic language
text:
4.7 Type-driven design in a dynamic language
Type-driven design means making domain concepts, admissible states, relationships, and operations explicit in the values and contracts from which the program is composed. Its goal is not to imitate a static typechecker. Its test is whether the representation retains knowledge and makes consumers simpler.
Use an iterative workflow:

Start from domain and consumers. Identify the decisions the program must make and the outputs, side effects, or external authorities involved.
Sketch representative nouns and verbs. Model a few important values, variants, containment relationships, and operations directly.
Inventory contracts. Record shape, cardinality, membership, presence, defaults, local constraints, and contextual requirements encountered in those sketches.
Place each rule. Use properties, classes, aggregates, or contextual operations according to information visibility.
Exercise the operations. Let methods expose missing distinctions, awkward variants, and laws the representation should preserve.
Extract repeated recipes. Generalize property or validator machinery only after real repetition, then revisit both nouns and verbs.







flowchart LR
  Domain["Domain pressures"] --> Sketch["Representative nouns and verbs"]
  Sketch --> Inventory["Property and contract inventory"]
  Inventory --> Placement["Place rules by information boundary"]
  Placement --> Operations["Exercise operations and laws"]
  Operations --> Refine["Refine distinctions and representations"]
  Refine --> Sketch
  Operations --> Extract["Extract repeated machinery"]




Figure 4.1: Type-driven design is an iterative loop between domain meaning, representation, and operations.





Figure 4.1 emphasizes that the model and its operations mature together; neither is a one-way derivation from the other.
The color example shows why the loop matters. Starting from the noun alone might produce a four-field class. Exercising as_hex(color) then forces a decision about rounding, alpha inclusion, and canonical case. Exercising blend(foreground, background) reveals that alpha is semantically different from the RGB channels and that the result should again satisfy the Color contract. Asking for faithful round trips may reveal a second concern—the original wire spelling—that should not be confused with domain equality. Each verb either confirms the representation or exposes knowledge it failed to retain.
Construction can then act as evidence for the invariants visible at that boundary. It is not a universal certificate: unsupported mutation, shared reference payloads, and external facts outside the validator’s view require their own contracts.

title: 4  Types and Meaning: Semantic Types, Structure, and Type-Driven Design
text:
4.8 Data-driven design, in two senses
“Data-driven” names two distinct and equally useful ideas, and conflating them causes confusion.
Design driven by data about the domain. Before abstracting, census the actual corpus: which shapes recur across a specification, which fields are required in practice, which enum values actually occur. Generalized machinery is then earned by observed repetition rather than speculation. A property-factory layer should contain the recipes real models reuse, not entries added “for completeness.” This restraint applies to infrastructure, not to naming an important concept that appears only once.
Behavior represented as data. Tables and specifications that drive computation: a classification table that generates both a style expression and a legend; a schedule that drives a state machine; quoted expressions composed into generated validator functions. This is the older Lisp/Unix sense — programs manipulating programs-as-data — and it reappears in Documents, Schemas, and Languages as the foundation of DSL and codegen work. When the specification is owned and semantic, validators, defaults, schemas, documentation, and interfaces can be deliberate projections from it. This removes independent definitions and makes agreement testable; it does not make generators infallible.
Candidate values show why retaining intent matters. A numeric vector alone does not say whether its elements are observations, bounds, or values to try during tuning. A CandidateValues concept can establish non-emptiness, element constraints, ordering or uniqueness policy, and the fact that the vector expresses a search choice. Once constructed, preparation and execution code no longer infer intent from length or naming conventions. Whether this concept is a validated property or a nominal class depends on whether it must travel independently or participate in dispatch.

title: 4  Types and Meaning: Semantic Types, Structure, and Type-Driven Design
section: 4.9 The wire universe versus the domain universe
text:
4.9 The wire universe versus the domain universe
Documents live in an impoverished type universe. JSON has exactly six kinds: null, boolean, number, string, array, object. R’s universe is richer and messier: NULL and NA (distinct!), integer versus double, length-one vectors standing in for scalars, named lists versus unnamed lists, attributes. Designing a document model means designing the mapping between universes, and most of the notorious bugs live in four mismatches:

Number: JSON does not distinguish 8 from 8L. If a property demands S7::class_integer, wire input and casual users will supply doubles. Either accept S7::class_numeric plus an integerish validator, or coerce in the admission function — but decide once for that boundary.
Scalar: JSON has scalars; R has length-one vectors. Every “string” property needs a length-1 law somewhere, which is why scalar-ness is usually the first check in any property-validator foundation.
Nothing: JSON can omit a key, or set it to null; R has NULL and also NA. These are up to four distinct meanings (“never mentioned,” “explicitly cleared,” “unknown,” “not applicable”) flowing through two representations. Tony Hoare called null references his billion-dollar mistake; R doubled the budget. The only defense is an explicit, per-property presence policy.
Empty: an empty array, an empty object, and an absent key serialize differently and often mean different things ("layers": [] versus no layers key). Serializers need a stated omit-empty policy per field.

For the running example, the domain may store a canonical Color(red, green, blue, alpha) while one wire format accepts "#336699", another accepts c(51, 102, 153, 1), and a third emits named fields. Admission functions can normalize all three into the domain value, and serializers can project it back into the chosen dialect. If exact lexical round-tripping matters—such as preserving "#369" rather than emitting "#336699"—the original spelling is additional provenance that must be stored explicitly. It cannot be recovered from the normalized color.

title: 4  Types and Meaning: Semantic Types, Structure, and Type-Driven Design
text:
4.10 Presence and default ownership
“Optional” conflates questions a property model should answer separately:

Must the resulting object contain the property?
Must the caller explicitly provide it?
May the stored value be NULL or NA?
Are a zero-length vector, empty string, list, or bag meaningful?
Does omission invoke a default?
Does serialization omit the field, emit null, or emit an empty value?
Who owns the default: R construction, an external authority, or a caller requesting later materialization?

A default should encode domain knowledge, not merely make construction stop complaining. Empty strings, zeroes, and sentinel values are not harmless when they mean “the model does not know”; they erase the distinction between omission and a meaningful value. If no lawful value follows from the domain, require the caller to supply one or represent absence explicitly.
Color makes default ownership visible. If the style language defines omitted alpha as fully opaque, alpha = 1 is domain knowledge and an R-owned default can record it immediately. If omission means “let the rendering engine choose,” storing 1 destroys a distinction the wire and runtime may care about. The model should then preserve omission—perhaps with NULL or a distinct deferred-default state—and materialize the value only when the authoritative engine or metadata is available. A convenient default is correct only when the model owns the choice.
The compact example is a document version restricted to 8. The document may require the field and always emit it, while the R constructor permits omission because it owns the default. The stored value may be non-null and restricted to one literal. Those statements are compatible: “required in the resulting document” does not imply “the caller must type it.” If wire input may contain 8, 8L, or another tolerated spelling, coercion belongs in the admission function; the literal property contract should judge only the canonical stored representation.
Collapsing these choices into optional = TRUE loses distinctions needed for patching, merging, and faithful round trips.
One S7 mechanic makes this especially concrete. In S7 0.2.2, a property with no explicit default receives the prototype of its declared class; for a union, that prototype comes from the union’s first member. Reordering a union can therefore change constructed values even though the set of accepted classes is unchanged. Treat member order as behavior when relying on the implicit default, or specify the default explicitly so order does not silently choose one.

title: 4  Types and Meaning: Semantic Types, Structure, and Type-Driven Design
text:
4.11 Literals, enums, and identity
A recurring puzzle when modeling specifications: a field whose value is fixed ("version": 8, "type": "geojson"). JSON Schema calls it const; TypeScript calls it a literal type. Three modeling options exist, and the choice is a genuine design decision, not a technicality:

Class identity. The field is not state at all; it is what the class is. Model it as a computed (getter-only) property or inject it at serialization. Two instances of the class can never differ on it, and it is not a constructor argument.
Stored with a default and a closed validator. The field is state that happens to have one lawful value today — the spec may add values, or round-tripping must preserve exactly what the wire said.
Boundary-normalized. Accept lenient input (8, 8L, even "8") at the admission boundary and store the canonical form.

The two questions that decide it: can two instances of this class ever differ on this value? (If no, it is identity, not state.) And must a round-trip preserve the user’s supplied value verbatim? (If yes, it must be stored.) Type discriminators in tagged unions (“this is a geojson source”) are often class identity — the class is the tag — while version fields are judgment calls that depend on whether one class will represent multiple spec versions.

title: 4  Types and Meaning: Semantic Types, Structure, and Type-Driven Design
text:
4.12 Refinements, for the statically minded
If you come from typed languages, the property validator is best understood as a runtime refinement type: { x : numeric | 0 <= x && x <= 255 }. The class system checks the base type; the refinement predicate narrows it. This framing explains the layering rule in Parse, Don’t Validate — base type and refinement are checked in that order, and S7 formalizes it by validating class before calling the property validator — and it explains why refinements should be pure and cheap: they run at every construction and replacement, like a type check would.

title: 5  Parse, Don’t Validate: Boundaries and Retained Knowledge
text:
5.1 Keep the result of checking
Alexis King’s “Parse, don’t validate” is not merely advice to check early (King 2019). It asks what representation remains after the check. A predicate can report that a value is acceptable and then discard the reason. A parser returns a value whose representation records what was established.
King’s contrast is usefully concrete. A function with the shape validateNonEmpty :: [a] -> () inspects a list, fails when it is empty, and returns no evidence when it succeeds. A later consumer receives the same [a] and must trust a convention or ask the same question again. parseNonEmpty :: [a] -> NonEmpty a performs the same inspection but returns a representation that retains the result. The important difference is not whether a check ran; it is whether the program kept what the check learned.
Two common pathologies follow when it does not. Shotgun parsing scatters recognition and rejection across the processing pipeline, so code begins acting on input before deciding what the input means and may discover a problem only after side effects or expensive work. Boolean blindness compresses a richer fact into TRUE or FALSE: the bit records that some predicate succeeded but carries neither the established structure nor the reason it matters. Both pathologies force downstream code to reconstruct knowledge the boundary already possessed.
In R, this is a runtime discipline rather than a compile-time proof:
An S7 object can therefore act as a construction certificate, but only within a stated boundary. It certifies:
It does not certify facts that require unavailable context, laws never encoded, or the future contents of reference-valued payloads. Low-level mutation, unchecked validation escape hatches, and a mutable environment stored inside an otherwise valid object can all invalidate stronger claims. A getter’s result also needs its own contract; a declared property class does not by itself prove arbitrary computed output.
The useful claim is consequently precise: consumers may rely on the invariants established by the supported construction and transformation paths. Package authors make that claim credible by keeping those paths small, documented, and tested.
The progression from a primitive to a domain value makes the claim tangible. A character string "#336699" is only text; a successful parse_color() can return a Color whose channels are canonical finite integers in the declared range. Code that accepts Color need not repeatedly parse the hex spelling or re-check those channel laws. The object acts as a certificate for exactly those bounded facts. It is not a proof that an arbitrary getter is correct, that reference-valued internals never changed, or that every target renderer supports the color. Those stronger claims belong to other boundaries.
S7’s deferred-validation escape hatches make the boundary especially worth stating precisely. The detailed behavior of S7::valid_eventually() and S7::valid_implicitly(), including the difference between final validation and no final validation, is developed in Chapter 2. Here the architectural conclusion is enough: supported construction and update paths preserve the advertised certificate; unchecked internal paths transfer the proof obligation to their caller.
