title: 5  Parse, Don’t Validate: Boundaries and Retained Knowledge
text:
5.3 Three different boundary decisions
Strict construction, tolerant parsing, and compilation answer different questions.
Strict construction creates a known domain value. RunSpecification() may require a bounded positive budget, a supported method, a valid candidate set, and a coherent relationship between its properties. Failure means no RunSpecification exists.
Tolerant parsing admits foreign or versioned input. It need not pretend that every input is known:

recognized and complete input becomes a known variant;
useful but unsupported input becomes an explicit UnknownSpecification;
incomplete input becomes a PartialSpecification carrying diagnostics;
input with no useful recoverable structure causes a condition.

Tolerance preserves knowledge only when uncertainty is represented. Returning a known class after silently dropping unknown fields is not tolerant parsing; it is lossy translation.
Compilation applies a target policy. A parser may preserve an unknown variant so that a document can be inspected or round-tripped, while compile_run() rejects it because the execution engine cannot assign it meaning. Parsing asks what can be represented; compilation asks what this target can execute.
This separation avoids two bad extremes: making every reader reject future content, and letting unknown content reach an executor as though it were understood.
The three decisions can form one continuous pipeline rather than three competing APIs. A tolerant reader first preserves what it can know. A strict constructor mints a RunSpecification only for a recognized, intrinsically lawful request. prepare() combines that specification with data and target context to produce PreparedRun, and execute() accepts only the prepared form. Unknown or partial parse variants remain inspectable and round-trippable, but compile_run() refuses them unless its target policy defines a lowering. Each arrow strengthens or preserves knowledge; none silently claims more than its inputs justify.

title: 5  Parse, Don’t Validate: Boundaries and Retained Knowledge
text:
5.4 Constructors normalize; validators verify
Boundary functions may accept several input spellings, normalize names, coerce values under an explicit policy, and attach diagnostics. Constructors for known classes then receive canonical property values.
Validators should verify those canonical values, not repeatedly parse them. A property validator handles local laws such as length, range, membership, or a pattern. It returns NULL on success or a character vector containing one or more problems. A class validator handles relationships among the properties it can see and likewise may return multiple problems.
That cardinality matters. Reporting several independent violations in one construction attempt can be useful, and S7 validators are not limited to one message.

title: 5  Parse, Don’t Validate: Boundaries and Retained Knowledge
5  Parse, Don’t Validate: Boundaries and Retained Knowledge
text:
5.6 Contextual preparation
Consider a computation request:
loose input
    -> RunSpecification
    -> prepare(specification, dataset)
    -> PreparedRun
    -> execute()
RunSpecification can establish intrinsic facts:

budget is a positive scalar within the package limit;
method is a supported value;
candidate values are represented explicitly rather than inferred from vector length;
local properties obey a cross-property rule.

It cannot establish that selected columns exist in a later dataset, that a candidate count fits the number of available features, or that case weights match the row count. Those requirements become checkable only when both the specification and dataset are present.
prepare() is therefore not a second constructor that repeats validation. It is a contextual operation that combines already-established intrinsic facts with dataset facts and returns a stronger value. PreparedRun can carry the resolved columns, normalized candidate plan, data fingerprint, and any diagnostics or provenance needed by execution.
This is the temporal rule demonstrated particularly clearly by the public design of rtemis: check as early as possible, as late as necessary. Declaration errors whose inputs are already available can fail when a property specification is created. Configuration errors can fail before an expensive training run. Data-bound requirements—candidate counts relative to features, selected names relative to columns, or weights relative to rows—must wait until the data exists, but should run immediately then. Deferral is not omission. The future requirement is declared early and discharged at the first boundary with enough information.
The downstream payoff is observable. execute() no longer:

rechecks scalar shape and local ranges;
guesses whether a vector denotes one value or several candidates;
repeatedly looks up or validates column names;
discovers an impossible request after expensive work has begun.

The representation records that preparation occurred. If the dataset can change, the contract must say whether PreparedRun owns a snapshot, records an identity/version to check, or must be rebuilt. Construction cannot certify an external resource forever.

title: 5  Parse, Don’t Validate: Boundaries and Retained Knowledge
text:
5.7 Supported transformations and cost
Property and class validators are hot-path code because supported property replacement revalidates. Keep them pure and inexpensive. Multi-property invariants require grouped replacement, such as S7::set_props(), so valid transitions are not rejected at an invalid intermediate state.
Bulk operations may defer validation and validate the final value once, but an unchecked path transfers the proof obligation to its caller. Such paths are implementation techniques, not public evidence of validity.
Every exported transformation should state its postcondition:

does it return another intrinsically valid RunSpecification?
does changing a context-sensitive field invalidate preparation?
does it preserve unknown foreign content?
can reference-valued contents change behind the object’s back?

Construction certificates remain useful only when their supported update paths preserve the advertised meaning.

title: 5  Parse, Don’t Validate: Boundaries and Retained Knowledge
text:
5.8 Conditions, diagnostics, and outcomes
Conditions and values serve different control-flow contracts.

Use classed conditions for contract violations, impossible requests, and failures that should unwind unless handled.
Store diagnostics on unknown or partial parse variants when callers need to inspect and preserve them as data.
Use an outcome family when success, rejection, cancellation, or failure is an expected result of a domain operation.

The conversion point should be explicit. A batch runner might catch selected conditions around one task and produce a TaskFailed outcome, while programmer errors continue to propagate. Chapter 5 defines the composition policy for those outcomes; merely defining variant classes does not decide whether failures short-circuit or accumulate.
The distinction is easiest to understand narratively. If a caller asks for a negative budget, no lawful request exists: the boundary signals a classed condition and unwinds. If a remote job was accepted but later timed out, TaskFailed may be an ordinary result that a batch report must retain beside completed tasks. A warning can describe a recoverable normalization, while a diagnostic attached to PartialSpecification explains preserved uncertainty. The same words—error, warning, failure—are not interchangeable channels. Choose according to the control-flow promise callers need, then provide one deliberate adapter where a selected condition becomes an outcome value.
For caller-facing conditions, cli::cli_abort() can provide structured, classed errors while rlang::caller_arg() and rlang::caller_env() preserve the user’s argument name and call context. Validator messages should remain short statements of violated laws.

title: 5  Parse, Don’t Validate: Boundaries and Retained Knowledge
6  Composition and Dispatch: Variants, Operations, and Outcomes
text:
6.1 Alternatives belong in the representation
A product combines fields: a task has an identifier, a request, and resource limits. A sum describes alternatives: execution finishes, is rejected, is cancelled, or fails with diagnostics.
Products are familiar because almost every record-shaped class is one: a Task contains an identifier and a request and resource limits. Sums are less visible in conventional object-oriented notation even though domains are full of them: a source is vector tiles or raster tiles or inline features; a response is success-with-a-value or failure-with-diagnostics. The two constructions answer different questions. Adding optional fields to a product does not turn it into an honest sum; it merely asks validators and consumers to recover the missing alternative structure.
Flattening alternatives into one record produces familiar warning signs: mode flags that reinterpret other fields, mutually exclusive nullable properties, and repeated switch() statements. When alternatives have different meaning, fields, or behavior, represent that distinction directly.
For example, a record with is_remote, nullable url, nullable data, and a type string invites rules such as “exactly one of url and data is set” and “ignore url unless is_remote.” A RemoteSource(url) / InlineSource(data) family makes the same facts structural. Similarly, a single status record with nullable value, reason, and error asks every consumer to repeat a switch(status) and remember which fields are legal. Concrete outcome variants move that switch into dispatch and give each alternative only the state it can actually carry.
S7 provides several related mechanisms, but they do different jobs.

title: 6  Composition and Dispatch: Variants, Operations, and Outcomes
text:
6.2 Five mechanisms, five responsibilities

6.2.1 Unions state accepted alternatives
S7::new_union() describes which classes a position accepts. Its members may be primitive classes, NULL, or domain classes:
CandidateSelection <- S7::new_union(
  FixedCandidate,
  CandidateSet
)
The union says that a property accepts either intent. It does not create a runtime variant, define shared fields, provide a dispatch target, or prove that all possible alternatives have been listed forever. Dispatch sees the class of the value, not “the union.”
Member order can also affect the prototype used for an unset property, so a union is not a neutral defaulting mechanism. Chapter 3 discusses that union-default caveat together with the separate questions of nullability, optionality, and default policy.
This candidate example preserves a distinction that a numeric vector loses: one fixed tuning value and several values to search are different requests even when both happen to contain one number.


6.2.2 Concrete classes preserve variant identity
FixedCandidate and CandidateSet are nominal values that can carry different invariants and methods. Use concrete variants when callers or operations must retain which alternative was chosen. A constrained string is enough when alternatives differ only by a tag and never by data or behavior.


6.2.3 Abstract parents provide shared schema or protocol
An abstract CandidateIntent parent can supply shared properties or serve as a dispatch position:
CandidateIntent <- S7::new_class(
  "CandidateIntent",
  abstract = TRUE
)
An abstract parent prevents construction of the parent itself. It does not seal the family, enumerate every child, or guarantee that methods exist for each child. Use inheritance for an honest is-a relationship and a useful dispatch axis; use composition for has-a relationships and independent axes.


6.2.4 Coverage tests check the family you claim to support
If a package publishes a known set of variants, keep that set explicit and test each required operation against it. The test is evidence about the registered family at that revision, not language-level exhaustiveness.
Open families need a conformance suite for extension classes. Closed-by-policy families need tests that fail when a new internal variant lacks an operation. Neither convention turns the hierarchy into a sealed type.
An open family also needs an evolution policy. Introduce a new verb with a loud parent fallback before making it required, publish the conformance suite for extension packages to run, and version the extension contract when a required operation or law must change. A third-party class can continue to construct after the protocol has evolved while lacking the new behavior; construction success is therefore not compatibility evidence.


6.2.5 Fallbacks reject unsupported runtime cases
A method on an abstract parent or broad class can issue a clear error when no specific implementation exists. This improves failure behavior. It is not coverage: a fallback can make every call dispatch while every new variant is still unsupported.
Keeping these roles separate prevents a fallback from being described as exhaustiveness, a parent from being described as a union, or a union from being treated as a domain value.

title: 6  Composition and Dispatch: Variants, Operations, and Outcomes
section: 6.3 Define the operation before its methods
text:
6.3 Define the operation before its methods
A generic is not a contract merely because it has a name. Define each operation in five parts:

Meaning: what domain verb does it represent?
Accepted concepts: which argument roles participate in dispatch, and which values are admissible?
Result: what class or outcome family is returned?
Failure policy: which failures are conditions, diagnostics, or result variants?
Laws: what relationships must all methods preserve?

For example, render(model, dialect) might have this contract:

render a semantic model without changing it;
accept a Model and a Dialect, dispatching on both;
return a RenderedDocument;
signal an unsupported model–dialect pair as a classed condition;
preserve model meaning under the documented parse/render equivalence.

Methods then implement that contract for (SelectModel, PostgresDialect), (SelectModel, SQLiteDialect), and other supported pairs. Multiple dispatch is appropriate because neither argument alone owns the interaction. It avoids placing a dialect switch() inside every model or a model switch() inside every dialect.
Coverage is a separate artifact from dispatch. Keep the supported model–dialect matrix explicit, test that every published pair has a specific method, and test that unsupported pairs reach the documented fallback. Adding a model, adding a dialect, and adding support for one pair are three different changes. In an open contract, a broad fallback keeps failure clear while a conformance suite tells extenders which pairs and laws they have actually implemented.
The operation should evolve before the method table does. A change from “render without semantic loss” to “render with target-specific approximation” changes the contract even if every method still returns a RenderedDocument. Name the approximation policy, diagnostics, and equivalence relation explicitly; otherwise method coverage can conceal semantic drift.
Single dispatch remains the usual choice when one concept controls the variation. Ordinary functions remain preferable when there is only one behavior and no extension point.

title: 6  Composition and Dispatch: Variants, Operations, and Outcomes
section: 6.4 Nouns and verbs expose each other’s gaps
text:
6.4 Nouns and verbs expose each other’s gaps
Representation and operations should be designed together.

If prepare() keeps asking whether a numeric vector means “fixed” or “search these,” the model is missing candidate intent.
If execute() branches on several nullable fields to infer what happened, the model is missing task-outcome variants.
If render() branches on both model and dialect tags, the design is missing a useful multiple-dispatch axis.
If a proposed class has no invariant, independent lifetime, or operation, it may be a property contract rather than a domain concept.

This is an iterative process: sketch representative classes and verbs, use the verbs to find missing distinctions, and extract repeated property machinery only after the distinctions are understood.

title: 6  Composition and Dispatch: Variants, Operations, and Outcomes
text:
6.5 Composition over inheritance
“Favor composition over inheritance” is primarily a warning about using a hierarchy for implementation reuse. A parent chosen merely to donate fields or helper behavior creates a nominal claim that dispatch will later treat as meaningful. It also couples children to parent details and forces independent dimensions into one tree, leading to combinations such as ColoredBorderedScrollableWindow.
S7 avoids some classic fragile-base-class mechanics because parents chiefly contribute property schema and dispatch positions, but the design rule remains. Inherit when a value honestly is a member of the parent concept and substitutability is useful: VectorSource is a Source. Compose when a value has a collaborator or an independent axis: a style has sources and layers; a shape has styling. Do not invent a parent because two classes happen to share property names.
Healthy hierarchies are consequently shallow: often one abstract concept and one level of concrete variants. An intermediate parent must pay twice—by adding honest shared schema and by being a useful dispatch target. Primitive inheritance has the same honesty test: subclass character only when the domain value really is text, not when squeezing a structured object into a string happens to be convenient.

title: 6  Composition and Dispatch: Variants, Operations, and Outcomes
6  Composition and Dispatch: Variants, Operations, and Outcomes
6  Composition and Dispatch: Variants, Operations, and Outcomes
6  Composition and Dispatch: Variants, Operations, and Outcomes
text:
6.9 Encapsulation and indirection
R’s openness makes the exported surface a convention rather than an access barrier. Constructors, generics, and invariant-preserving transformations are the supported front door. The guarantees in Chapter 4 are promises about that door, not about arbitrary internal modification.
This is Parnas-style information hiding: hide decisions likely to change, not data out of a desire for secrecy. If property layout is expected to evolve, expose stable generics rather than making documented @ paths the primary interface. When another ecosystem requires $ access, S3 behavior, or a legacy shape, put a thin facade in front of one S7 source of truth. Duplicating mutable state on both sides creates two authorities and defeats the facade.
Dispatch ownership clarifies plugin design. When your package owns a generic and another package owns a class, registration is an extension point: a provider package can add its class and methods without editing the generic’s package. When your package owns the class and another ecosystem owns the generic, registration is integration. S7::super() makes intentional parent delegation explicit instead of relying on an implicit next-method search. The public sqlr design illustrates the two-dimensional case: render_sql(x, con) varies with both the semantic object and the connection dialect, so one method owns each meaningful pair.
Indirection earns its place when it absorbs a real variation:

a generic absorbs behavior across meaningful classes;
multiple dispatch absorbs a genuine interaction between concepts;
a semantic class preserves intent that a primitive would erase;
a projection absorbs change between a model and an external form.

Do not require three instances before naming an important domain concept. Apply repetition thresholds to generalized factories and framework machinery, not to distinctions such as candidate intent or task outcome that consumers already need.
Every layer should nevertheless pay rent by absorbing a real axis of variation. A generic pays by supporting meaningful behavioral variation or a real extension contract. A semantic class pays by preserving intent and laws a primitive would erase. A projection pays by isolating transport churn. A wire-name map pays by keeping foreign naming out of the domain model.
A wrapper with no law or operation, an interface with one implementation and no extension pressure, or a factory abstracting one construction does not pay that rent. Parnas’s hiding, facades, and “composition over inheritance” are not demands for more layers; they are tools for placing the few layers whose variation and authority can be named.

title: 7  Documents, Schemas, and Languages: Authority at the Wire
text:
7.1 A document model is a contract between representations
Map styles, configuration files, database schemas, and query trees are declarative values consumed by another system. A useful model identifies:
A root can certify unique names and resolvable references only when it sees the complete collection. It cannot certify behavior owned by a renderer, database, or version of an external specification. Chapter 4’s invariant visibility rule applies at the wire as well as inside ordinary values.
This recurring anatomy is worth making explicit. Composition edges form an ownership tree: a style contains sources and layers, or a catalog contains collections and items. Symbolic references add a second graph over that tree: a layer names a source, and an item links to a collection. Those references behave like foreign keys. Their uniqueness and resolution laws belong to the aggregate root, the lowest object that can see both definitions and uses. That root is naturally the unit of consistency, mutation, and serialization.
Boundary constructors complete the pattern by lifting objects users already have into document nodes. The public stacbuildr API, for example, provides constructors such as item_from_terra() and item_from_sf() rather than requiring users to transcribe raster and geometry metadata into nested lists. The constructor interprets the native object once, normalizes it, and enters the document model through its supported front door.

title: 7  Documents, Schemas, and Languages: Authority at the Wire
7  Documents, Schemas, and Languages: Authority at the Wire
text:
7.2 Documents as programs, within limits
A declarative document can often be treated as a program for another system: a map style is interpreted by a rendering engine, a SQL model by a database, and a query tree by a compiler. The package that builds it then resembles a front end. It parses convenient inputs, constructs a structured representation, checks the static facts it owns, and renders once at the boundary. This analogy explains why string templating is weak: strings erase the structure on which local checks and transformations depend.
The analogy is bounded, however. A STAC item is also an interchange record, and a configuration document may chiefly be persisted data. The package may preserve a foreign language without interpreting it, and the external engine still owns runtime behavior and full conformance. Calling every serializer a compiler would obscure those authority limits. Use the compiler vocabulary when semantic lowering or target policy is real; otherwise parser, adapter, and serializer are more accurate names.
There is no single correct relationship between an S7 model and a schema. Four architectures recur.

title: 7  Documents, Schemas, and Languages: Authority at the Wire
text:
7.3 Four schema and model architectures

1. External-schema container2. Generated transport facade3. Hand-designed semantic model4. Owned semantic specification with projections


An external schema owns the content contract. The package validates a foreign document with the schema’s tooling, then stores or wraps the resulting list-like content for navigation and extension.
This architecture fits heterogeneous schemas supplied at runtime or systems whose main job is schema-mediated transport. The S7 properties may describe the wrapper and schema machinery while the external schema describes the contained entries. Editing arbitrary nested content does not automatically preserve conformance unless edits pass through another validation boundary.
Its advantage is fidelity to an authority that can change independently. Its cost is a deliberately weak semantic core: navigation and preservation may be available while domain dispatch and invariant-rich transformations are not. It works best when the package is a transport or validation tool rather than an alternate implementation of the foreign language.


An external schema or interface definition generates classes, field maps, or serializers that mirror the wire. This is appropriate when faithful coverage of a large, changing transport surface is itself the requirement.
Generated transport classes should be named and documented as transport types. They absorb foreign naming and version churn; an adapter can translate the subset with domain meaning into a hand-designed model. Generation does not establish semantics absent from the source, and generated code can still contain generator bugs. Test it against the external contract.
This is an anti-corruption layer, not a claim that two class graphs should remain isomorphic forever. Regenerate the transport side when the foreign schema changes; evolve the semantic side when the package’s concepts change. The adapter is where version differences, omission policy, and unsupported foreign constructs become explicit.


The model is organized around concepts and operations rather than wire objects. It may combine several foreign fields into one semantic value, split one foreign object into several concepts, or omit incidental structure.
This architecture earns its cost when nominal identity, invariants, generic operations, or multiple targets matter. The external schema remains evidence and a boundary authority, not the class diagram. Translation is often an adapter or compiler rather than a faithful conversion.
Because it organizes around meaning, this model can be smaller than the wire surface and deeper where operations need it. The trade-off is an explicit translation burden: losses, preservation of unknown fields, and the equality relation for round trips can no longer be assumed from structural similarity.


The package owns an inspectable semantic specification from which it derives some combination of classes, validators, schemas, documentation, interfaces, and renderers.
This is stronger than reflecting arbitrary validator closures. Only explicitly represented knowledge can be projected reliably: a declaration carrying minimum, maximum, membership, presence, and default policy can be inspected; an opaque function may enforce the same rule without exposing it. Generated projections can still disagree because translators can be incomplete or wrong. Shared declarations remove independent definitions and make agreement testable; they do not guarantee agreement for free.
Generation from an owned semantic specification is different from mirroring incidental foreign structure. The former can legitimately produce native domain classes when the specification actually contains their meaning.
This architecture is appropriate when a package truly owns the declaration and several consumers need it. A property specification might project to an S7 validator, JSON Schema, documentation, and a form. The declaration reduces independent definitions, but every projector remains code that can be incomplete or wrong. Cross-projection agreement tests are therefore part of the architecture, not optional reassurance.



These architectures can coexist. A package may receive an external transport document, preserve its unknown fields, adapt known content into a semantic model, and render that model through projections derived from an owned specification.

title: 7  Documents, Schemas, and Languages: Authority at the Wire
text:
7.4 The roles of external authority
An external authority can participate in at least three ways.
Wire gate. An official schema or validator decides whether input or output conforms to a published format. This is a boundary check, not a replacement for domain invariants.
Runtime metadata provider. A database catalog, driver registry, or remote capability endpoint supplies allowed values and limits only after context is known. Preparation resolves a request against that metadata, much like prepare(specification, dataset) in Chapter 4.
Test oracle. An independent parser, renderer, or validator checks generated artifacts in tests. It can reveal disagreement without becoming the package’s in-memory representation.
State which role applies. “The schema is authoritative” is incomplete unless readers know whether it governs wire acceptance, dynamic capabilities, test comparison, or all three.

title: 7  Documents, Schemas, and Languages: Authority at the Wire
section: 7.5 Typed and open are per-node choices
text:
7.5 Typed and open are per-node choices
Typing depth should follow the guarantees and operations required at each node.

Use a typed class where node identity, invariants, references, or dispatch matter.
Use a validated open bag where keys are intentionally extensible but local shape rules still matter.
Keep an embedded language opaque when the package only preserves it.
Use a typed AST only when inspection, transformation, or multi-target compilation requires node semantics.

A document can therefore have a typed root and typed reference-bearing nodes, an open metadata bag, and opaque expression payloads. “Typed document” need not mean that every leaf has a class; “open document” need not mean that nothing is checked.
Every open bag should state its guarantees: key syntax, value types, duplicate policy, recursion limits, and whether unknown entries survive rendering.

title: 7  Documents, Schemas, and Languages: Authority at the Wire
text:
7.6 Parser, adapter, compiler, and conversion
Name a translation according to its contract.
A parser interprets external syntax or loose data and returns known, unknown, or partial document variants with diagnostics. It owns syntax, version gating, normalization, and unknown-key policy.
An adapter maps between existing representations under an explicit policy. It may be contextual or lossy, but it does not imply that one representation is source code for the other.
A compiler translates a semantic model into a target representation and applies target policy. It may reject a model that parsed successfully, lower one node into many target nodes, or report unsupported features.
S7::convert() is best reserved for faithful representation changes with a clear source and target class. A contextual, diagnostic-producing, lossy, or one-to-many translation deserves a named function.
A serializer projects an accepted in-memory representation to a wire shape. A to_wire() method owns wire names, required type tags and version constants, omission versus explicit null, ordering or canonicalization policy, recursive descent, and preservation of declared extension content.
Its inverse, from_wire(), is a parser rather than object restoration by fiat. It owns syntax decoding, version gates, coercion to canonical values, unknown-key handling, migrations, diagnostics, and construction through the current front door. Keeping those responsibilities in one pair prevents wire knowledge from leaking into constructors, mutators, and render methods throughout the class graph.
For each translation, document:

what meaning and foreign content are preserved;
what is normalized or deliberately lost;
which context and target policy are applied;
what diagnostics can be produced;
which equality relation defines success.

Do not introduce a shared intermediate representation merely by taking the union of several foreign formats. An IR is earned when multiple real inputs or outputs reveal stable shared semantics.

title: 7  Documents, Schemas, and Languages: Authority at the Wire
text:
7.7 Round trips require named equivalence
Two directions usually need different laws.
For a semantic model:
parse(render(model, dialect), dialect) ≈ model
For a foreign document:
render(parse(document), dialect) ≈ document
The symbol ≈ must be defined. Possible relations include:

exact representation identity, such as identical();
canonical equality after normalization;
semantic equivalence that ignores non-meaningful order or generated names;
wire equivalence after defaults and omission rules are resolved;
preservation equivalence that additionally requires unknown extensions to survive.

Most semantic document models promise canonical or semantic equivalence, not exact identity. A reflected database model may omit engine-specific details; a renderer may choose canonical whitespace; a parser may resolve defaults. Those can be sound round trips if the promised equivalence names the losses.
Reflection is also bounded. It reports what the external system exposes and what the reflector understands; it does not reconstruct every original authoring decision. Tests should compare within that declared observation boundary.
The public typedjson package offers a concrete round-trip design. For a supported value x, it tests identical(json_read(json_write(x, path)), x). Ordinary values keep ordinary JSON spellings—1L becomes 1, while the double 1 becomes 1.0—and only information JSON cannot carry is annotated. Thus NA_real_ receives a typed tag, character() records its empty-vector type, and an S7 object records the class identity needed to find current class code when reading. The worked point is not that every public format should preserve all R values. It is that the format states an exact equivalence, adds machinery only for distinctions needed by that equivalence, and tests the law over generated as well as curated values.

title: 7  Documents, Schemas, and Languages: Authority at the Wire
section: 7.8 Native serialization is not a durable wire contract
text:
7.8 Native serialization is not a durable wire contract
saveRDS() is useful for trusted, version-bound caches and test fixtures. It is a poor default for a public or long-lived interchange format. S7 currently serializes the class specification with each object, so an object can retain an older class definition after package code evolves. R’s serialization version identifies the stream format; it does not migrate domain classes (Vaughan 2024; R Core Team 2026).
Native serialization is also a trust boundary. R versions before 4.4.0 were affected by CVE-2024-27322 (National Vulnerability Database 2024; CERT Coordination Center 2024), and current RDS files can still contain executable or session-bound objects. Do not accept untrusted RDS as inert data. Prefer a bounded plain-data format, an explicit schema version, and current-code parsing and migration. When RDS is deliberately used as a cache, record relevant versions, constrain its source, and make cache invalidation cheaper than heroic migration.

title: 7  Documents, Schemas, and Languages: Authority at the Wire
text:
7.11 Embedded languages and safe generation
Use the shallowest representation that serves the consumers:

opaque data for pass-through;
constructor functions that build a target form;
typed AST nodes and separate compiler passes for analysis or multiple targets.

Code generation should likewise follow represented knowledge. Enum catalogs, wire-name maps, repetitive transport fields, and projections from an owned semantic specification are good candidates. Domain distinctions absent from the source still require design.
Generated validators, classes, schemas, and documentation need direct tests. Inspectability helps debugging but does not prove equivalence. Never evaluate untrusted document content as R code; keep unknown extensions inert, and bound the depth and size of recursive input before walking it.
The ladder becomes concrete in query systems. At the opaque rung, a package stores a SQL fragment or foreign expression and promises only to preserve it. At the combinator rung, functions such as select(), filter(), or expr_match() build a valid target-shaped tree without giving every node a domain class. At the typed-AST rung, node identity supports independent analysis and compilation passes. The public quickr project takes this deeper route for typed R-to-Fortran translation, while dbplyr builds relational expressions and lowers them to database-specific SQL. Their depth is justified because analysis and multi-target translation are part of the product; a pass-through field with one renderer would not earn the same machinery.

title: 7  Documents, Schemas, and Languages: Authority at the Wire
text:
7.12 Metaprogramming guardrails
R makes small languages easy to build, so generated checks and classes need stricter design discipline, not less. Checks as data can be useful when quoted, composable conditions are assembled into one inspectable validator. The generated function should print as ordinary understandable code and be tested directly. Splicing language objects created inside the package is appropriate; eval(parse(paste0(...))) and evaluation of document-supplied text are not.
Classes as data are equally legitimate because S7 classes are first-class values. A table can generate a regular family of enum or transport classes. Generation should stop where per-class meaning begins: if most generated classes need exceptions, readable hand-written definitions are the better model. In both patterns, generate structural regularity, keep inputs trusted, and test the generated artifact rather than only the factory.
