title: 8  Ecosystem Field Guide: Design Questions in Practice
text:
8.1 How can one declaration serve several consumers?
This guide is organized by decisions, not package inventory. Each exhibit is public and reader-verifiable, and each is evidence for a bounded design claim rather than a recommendation to copy a package wholesale.

title: 8  Ecosystem Field Guide: Design Questions in Practice
text:
8.1.1 rtemis: property contracts as inspectable data
rtemis treats a property declaration as more than a validator closure. Its public PropertySpec implementation retains value type, container shape, bounds, choices, defaults, null behavior, tuning intent, conditional applicability, and data-dependent bounds as data. That choice is causal: once the declaration can be inspected, the package can use the same facts to build executable S7 properties, establish defaults, project schemas and interfaces, and prepare a configuration against training data. A closure alone could enforce a value locally, but it could not explain the rule to those other consumers.
The distinction between a value and a candidate set shows why the extra model matters. Shape is not enough: a length-two vector might be one value, a range, or a search space. By recording tuning intent independently, PropertySpec prevents downstream code from reverse-engineering semantics from shape. Similarly, a data-dependent bound remains declared with the property even though it cannot be resolved until the training data supplies the missing context. Declaration and enforcement can therefore happen at different times without becoming different rules.
This concentration of knowledge creates obligations. A default should satisfy its own declaration; incompatible metadata axes should fail when the property is defined; and generated validators, schemas, and interfaces need alignment tests. Contract-as-data removes independently maintained definitions, not the possibility of a faulty projection. Nor does it make every rule reversible: reconstruction is credible only for the vocabulary that the declaration actually records.
Decision test. Use contract-as-data when several real consumers need the same facts and their agreement can be tested. A handwritten S7::new_property() remains simpler when construction is the only consumer.

title: 8  Ecosystem Field Guide: Design Questions in Practice
section: 8.2 Which objects are values, snapshots, or runtime owners?
text:
8.2 Which objects are values, snapshots, or runtime owners?

8.2.1 deputy: portable definitions at a permission boundary
deputy runs tasks with an ellmer chat and R tools. Its public documentation separates declarative configuration from a live run: tool definitions, permission policies, and usage limits describe requested behavior, while the Agent owns execution, streaming, counters, and host interaction. AgentResult records how a completed run ended, including stop reason and usage information.
The split follows ownership. Definitions and policies can travel as data because they do not themselves contain a live model connection or grant a capability. At execution time, the host binds symbolic tools and applies its permission policy; valid configuration is therefore not confused with authority. The running agent needs identity because it coordinates changing state and effects, while its completed result can become a value-like fact. Deputy also composes with ellmer’s public tool and structured-output meanings instead of inventing parallel ones, keeping package policy at the layer that owns it.
Read-only result fields, where used, express the lifecycle of completed facts. They are not evidence that every S7 value should be read-only. Editable configuration can retain value semantics and invariant-preserving replacement.
Decision test. Choose a reference owner for shared identity, live resources, or an observable lifecycle. Use values for portable definitions and completed facts, and keep requested capability distinct from host-granted authority.

title: 8  Ecosystem Field Guide: Design Questions in Practice
section: 8.3 When is a semantic middle representation worth its cost?
text:
8.3 When is a semantic middle representation worth its cost?

8.3.1 sqlr: one model for rendering, reflection, and comparison
sqlr supplies a representation of a database schema that is neither SQL text nor a live connection. Constructors create that model; dialect objects render it; sqlr_reflect() reconstructs it from a catalog; and sqlr_equal() and sqlr_diff() compare its meaning. These are independent consumers, so the schema model prevents each operation from re-parsing text or inventing a private account of tables and constraints.
The model also makes policy visible. Rendering can order tables by dependency and defer cycle-closing foreign keys to later statements. Dialects carry engine-specific behavior without requiring a live connection, and the package deliberately declines to offer an untested “ANSI SQL” fallback. Reflection is bounded by what a database exposes, so missing catalog facts remain documented limits instead of guessed values. Comparison can then ignore incidental constraint order or generated names and report differences in domain terms.
The resulting round-trip law is semantic, not textual: rendering into a particular engine and reflecting back should preserve the modeled meaning that engine can represent. Exact representation, canonical form, and domain equality remain separate claims. The public generic definitions at revision 8325581 make that operation vocabulary inspectable.


8.3.2 Additional exhibit: quickr’s typed compiler IR
quickr gives an IR a different reason to exist. Its R-to-Fortran compiler reads an in-language type declaration, lowers source through typed objects, and passes those objects between analysis and code-generation stages; the public quick.R source shows compiled artifacts such as FortranSubroutine being consumed as structured values. A typed IR is justified here because translation and analysis are the product. For a single textual rewrite, the same class graph would be ceremony.
Decision test. Introduce an intermediate representation after at least two consumers need the same stable meaning. Rendering alone may need an adapter; rendering plus reflection and comparison, or analysis plus code generation, can justify a shared typed model.

title: 8  Ecosystem Field Guide: Design Questions in Practice
section: 8.4 Who owns the contract: S7 properties or an external schema?
text:
8.4 Who owns the contract: S7 properties or an external schema?

8.4.1 S7schema: an externally validated container
S7schema validates YAML configuration against JSON Schema using AJV through V8. S7 classes supply the surrounding configuration and extension machinery, while detailed domain entries remain list content whose contract belongs to the external schema. This avoids translating every foreign rule into a second property system and keeps conformance with the authority that other implementations can share.
The cost is a wider gap between manipulation and certification. Arbitrary list editing does not automatically preserve validity, so an API must say which boundaries revalidate and which operations merely rearrange content. External authority removes duplicate rules only if consumers continue to consult it.


8.4.2 stacbuildr: native boundary constructors plus conformance
stacbuildr makes the other trade-off. It gives STAC catalogs, collections, and items native classes, projects them into familiar tabular or spatial forms, and validates emitted documents against published STAC schemas. Its item_from_terra(), item_from_sf(), and item_from_lidr() constructors translate objects users already hold while extracting spatial metadata. The native layer is useful because R-side construction, navigation, and projection need nominal concepts; the external validator remains useful because STAC, not the R package, owns wire conformance.
The contrast is not “schema versus classes.” S7schema keeps detailed entries under external-schema authority because the container and extension machinery are the main R-side concern. stacbuildr adds a semantic layer because its major nodes have operations in R, but still refuses to make that layer the sole judge of an external specification. In both designs, authority follows the knowledge rather than the implementation language.


8.4.3 Additional exhibit: typedjson’s minimal annotations
typedjson addresses a narrower authority problem: JSON cannot express every distinction among R values. Its public design at revision 7160c06 keeps ordinary values as ordinary JSON and adds annotations only where the wire format would otherwise lose information. Ordinary numeric spellings can preserve integer versus double (1 versus 1.0); annotations carry distinctions such as typed missing or empty values, non-finite numbers, attributes, and object-system metadata. The round-trip goal determines the annotations; it does not justify turning the whole document into an opaque serialization envelope. This is a useful minimum-metadata rule whenever readability and fidelity compete.
Decision test. Ask whether downstream operations need nominal identity and invariants inside R. If not, a validated external-schema container may suffice. If they do, add a semantic layer while retaining the external conformance oracle. Annotate a wire form only for distinctions its native vocabulary cannot preserve.

title: 8  Ecosystem Field Guide: Design Questions in Practice
section: 8.5 Should failure be a condition or a value?
text:
8.5 Should failure be a condition or a value?

8.5.1 resultr: explicit outcome sequencing
resultr defines an abstract Result parent with Success and Failure variants. Its Result.R implementation provides inspection, unwrapping, defaults, and and_then(). A Success applies the next computation; a Failure returns itself, making short-circuiting part of the protocol rather than a convention repeated by each caller.
The same source makes the condition/value boundary explicit. wrap_in_result() maps ordinary values to Success, errors and warnings to Failure, and existing results to themselves; and_then() uses rlang::try_fetch() at that boundary. This adapter matters because R conditions and result values serve different traffic. Conditions support immediate non-local control flow. Outcome values can be stored, inspected, combined, or returned through an ordinary value channel.
The exhibit therefore supports a choice, not a universal replacement for conditions. Programmer errors and failures requiring immediate unwinding still belong in the condition channel. A result protocol must also say whether failures short-circuit or accumulate; resultr demonstrates the former, while validation systems often need the latter.
Decision test. Choose the channel per subsystem, then define one deliberate adapter. Do not alternate ad hoc between thrown conditions and returned failures.

title: 8  Ecosystem Field Guide: Design Questions in Practice
section: 8.6 How much behavior belongs in a reusable contract?
text:
8.6 How much behavior belongs in a reusable contract?

8.6.1 Additional exhibit: s7contract’s executable laws
s7contract separates several strengths of agreement. Its public README at revision 41dce50 describes structural interfaces as named sets of required generics, explicit traits with registration and defaults, runtime argument and return checks, and generative laws with generators and shrinking. Method availability can show that an object has the required vocabulary; executable laws probe whether implementations preserve behavioral promises that a dispatch table cannot express.
The causal lesson is that “implements” has layers. Structural conformance is cheap and queryable, runtime contracts can localize bad inputs or outputs, and generative laws can be reused by third-party implementations. None supplies a compile-time proof, and sampled laws do not establish a theorem. Their value is to turn otherwise prose-only obligations into public, repeatable tests.
Decision test. Add reusable conformance laws when independent implementations share behavior important enough to test. Do not mistake method presence or generated examples for proof of all valid inputs.

title: 8  Ecosystem Field Guide: Design Questions in Practice
section: 8.7 When should policy become a composable object?
text:
8.7 When should policy become a composable object?

8.7.1 Additional exhibit: optimizers7 and parameters7
optimizers7 and parameters7 extract mathematical policies that modeling packages often bury inside loops and parameterizations. The public optimizers7 design models an optimizer separately from its stopping rule. Because “finished” is an independent policy, users can compose or replace stopping criteria without forking the algorithm. The parameters7 design models constrained parameters as reusable maps with inverses and derivatives, so an optimizer or likelihood can depend on a stable mathematical interface instead of one package’s private encoding.
This decomposition pays when behavior varies independently and has operations of its own. A tolerance used by exactly one loop may remain an argument. A stopping rule that combines criteria, or a parameter map that must be evaluated, inverted, and differentiated, has earned nominal identity and dispatch. Both packages also keep their abstractions narrow: optimization need not know what an observation is, and a parameter map need not own a statistical model.
Decision test. Promote policy to an object when it varies independently, composes with peers, or supports a reusable operation vocabulary. Keep a scalar option as data when no consumer needs those capabilities.

title: 8  Ecosystem Field Guide: Design Questions in Practice
text:
8.8 Cross-case synthesis
Across these cases, S7 is valuable less as a syntax for records than as a way to put authority and variation in inspectable places. rtemis centralizes facts because several projections need them. sqlr and quickr introduce middle representations because several transformations share stable semantics. S7schema and stacbuildr keep external specifications authoritative even when R-side objects add ergonomics. resultr names a control protocol, s7contract names conformance obligations, and optimizers7 makes an independently varying policy composable.
The recurring limit is equally important. Central metadata needs projection tests; an IR needs multiple substantive consumers; a native document model does not supersede its wire specification; a result value does not replace all conditions; generated laws are evidence rather than proof; and a policy object must earn its indirection. These are not package-specific cautions. They are the costs created by the same design moves that provide the benefit.

title: 8  Ecosystem Field Guide: Design Questions in Practice
section: 8.9 Questions to carry into a design
text:
8.9 Questions to carry into a design

How many consumers need the same declared knowledge?
Is this object a portable value, completed snapshot, or live owner?
Does a middle representation have more than one substantive consumer?
Is contract authority local, external, or shared through tested projections?
What equality relation makes a round trip meaningful?
Does failure control execution immediately, or travel as data?
Is a behavior merely configurable, or independently composable?
Which unknown content is rejected, preserved inertly, or interpreted?

S7 earns its place when nominal meaning, invariant placement, or generic operations simplify consumers—not merely because structured data exists.

title: 9  Doctrine: Principles, Decision Guides, and Named Anti-Patterns
text:
9.1 Principles
This document compresses the preceding argument into principles, decision guides, and named anti-patterns for design reviews. Each principle is framed by its downstream payoff: knowledge belongs in the model when it removes interpretation, checking, or branching from consumers.
A register note before the principles: everything in this document is doctrine — deliberately imperative defaults distilled from documented S7 behavior and observed ecosystem practice, but laws of neither. The imperative mood is a choice: a crisp default you can overrule for stated reasons is more useful in a design session than a hedge you can ignore. “Always” and “never” here mean “strong default,” and when a principle collides with a real constraint, the earlier documents carry the reasoning needed to make the trade explicitly.
Model meaning through representative designs. Begin with the domain, intended consumers, and a few representative values and operations. Record the semantic atoms and laws those examples expose, then revisit both structure and behavior. Meaning can be more stable than document shape, but it is discovered iteratively rather than by completing a universal foundation first.
Let construction retain evidence. Boundary functions turn loose input into representations that record what was learned, so downstream code can demand those representations instead of re-checking raw contents. Construction certifies only invariants visible at that boundary and preserved by supported transformations; references inside an object and external facts remain outside that certificate.
Constructors normalize; validators verify; boundaries translate. Coercion, canonicalization, and version gating happen once, at the boundary. Validators judge canonical values only, and stay pure and cheap because they run on every property write. A validator accommodating multiple input shapes is a parser in the wrong place, running forever.
Give every invariant one authoritative home. Place each law at the lowest boundary that sees everything it mentions: external conformance at the wire, parsing at the boundary, type on the property class, local law in the property validator, cross-property law in the class validator, cross-object law in the aggregate root, operation legality in the mutator, developer invariants in assertions. Each rung assumes the rungs below and duplicates none. A cheap duplicate deliberately retained for better boundary diagnostics is a documented trade; a law found on two rungs by accident is a bug waiting to be two different laws. The governing test is the rule’s visibility horizon. A channel range is visible to one property; start-before-end needs the whole object; unique ids need the collection; authorization needs the live authority. Below that horizon the rule is uncheckable, while above it the rule runs too often and couples code to context it does not need.
Treat presence and default ownership as a contract. Required in the result, caller-supplied, nullable, NA-able, empty, defaulted, and omitted on serialization are separate decisions. Record whether R, an external authority, or the caller requesting materialization owns a default. One optional flag cannot preserve these meanings.
Treat constants as identity when instances cannot differ. If two instances of a class can never differ on a field, the field is part of what the class is: model it as a computed property or inject it at serialization, and keep it out of the constructor. Store it only when round-trip fidelity or spec evolution demands that instances carry it.
Represent alternatives as alternatives. Flag fields, mutually exclusive nullables, and mode strings are sum types flattened into products. Give variants honest representation: concrete variant classes when identity, fields, or behavior differ; enum properties when only the tag differs; unions when one slot accepts several primitive or domain classes. Abstract parents provide shared schema or protocol but do not seal a family. Loud fallbacks and coverage tests detect unsupported known cases; they do not prove exhaustiveness.
Inherit for dispatch and substitutability; compose for structure. Parents contribute a property schema and a dispatch position to things that genuinely are the parent. Everything else — nesting, reuse, independent dimensions — is composition. Hierarchies stay shallow: abstract root, concrete leaves, intermediate levels only when they add a genuine is-a concept and either a useful dispatch position, shared invariant-bearing schema, or structural exclusion of illegal states. Inherit from a base type only when the object is that primitive.
Co-design nouns and verbs. Behavior belongs to generics, and interfaces are generic sets plus laws. Design the verb vocabulary as deliberately as the class graph. An extension point is a set of generics an implementor must support and the laws those methods must satisfy — write the laws down, executably where possible. Let operations revise the representation when they reveal missing distinctions. Reach for multiple dispatch when behavior genuinely varies along two type axes.
Choose lifecycle policy explicitly. Editable values are revised through replacement. Read-only snapshots are values whose public API forbids revision. Reference owners coordinate shared identity, resources, or observable lifecycles. Keep domain knowledge in values where possible, and document any reference-valued payload because outer validation will not observe its internal mutation.
These policies answer different questions. A value says that revision produces another value. A snapshot says that the represented fact is complete and the public API offers no revision, even though S7 replacement machinery still exists underneath. An owner says that aliases must observe one evolving process or resource. A chat may therefore own a live stream while emitting completed turns as snapshots; the hybrid is explicit rather than an exception hidden inside a nominally immutable object.
Revise related properties together, through the front door. Invariants spanning several properties imply every update of those properties goes through one grouped replacement (S7::set_props()), wrapped in a transformation function. Guarantees hold for supported clients of the exported surface; make the front door the easiest path.
Use one authoritative meaning with deliberate projections. When several outputs encode the same knowledge — an expression and a legend; a class graph and its documentation; a wire format and a pretty printer — designate one canonical source and derive deliberate projections. This removes independently maintained definitions and makes consistency testable; translators and generators can still be wrong.
Keep property access cheap and pure. Getters compute derivations; they never perform I/O, never mutate, never surprise. The moment x@thing can be slow or effectful, the object stops being data in the reader’s mind, and the whole value-semantics reasoning collapses.
Make generalized machinery earn its keep. Every layer of indirection pays rent by absorbing a demonstrated axis of variation. Apply the rule of three to factories, metamodels, and framework layers, not to naming an important domain concept. Delete machinery that no longer simplifies its consumers.
Choose schema authority before generation strategy. Validate against external schemas with the schema ecosystem’s own tools at the wire; read foreign schemas as a census that can inform a hand-designed semantic model. Generating a native transport facade may be appropriate when foreign flatness is authoritative. When the package owns a semantic specification, generating classes, validators, schemas, and documentation from it may also be appropriate. Do not confuse either case with mirroring incidental foreign structure without a consumer-driven reason.
The key distinction is between a transport facade and a semantic model. A facade may intentionally preserve foreign names, optionality, and nesting because exact interchange is its job. A semantic model collapses structural duplicates, names domain distinctions, and serves native operations. Some packages need both, joined by an explicit parser or adapter; generation is then a maintenance technique, not evidence that the two layers mean the same thing.
Refuse to guess. Where no correct behavior is known, an error beats a default. sqlr states the reason perfectly in declining to ship an “ANSI SQL” fallback dialect: an untestable default “would quietly accumulate behaviour no database had ever accepted.” The same logic condemns silent coercion of ambiguous input, fallback branches for “unknown type,” and any code path no test can exercise against a real authority. A loud, early error is information; a guess is deferred corruption.
Check as early as the inputs allow, as late as the context requires. The value of a check is proportional to the cost of the work it gates. Declarations should validate themselves at package load (a default violating its own bounds is the author’s bug, catchable before any user exists); configurations should validate fully before the expensive run they configure; and laws that mention context not yet in hand — data dimensions, live resources — should be declared at construction and checked in one named pass at the moment the context arrives, never guessed at and never skipped.
Design failure representation and composition separately. Conditions suit contract violations and control flow that should stop. Computational result values suit expected success or failure that callers compose as data. Domain outcome families describe events such as denied authority, cancellation, or completion. For each subsystem, separately specify whether failures short-circuit or accumulate, which diagnostics survive, and where conditions become values or values become conditions.
A computational result answers “did this calculation produce a value?” and usually carries mechanics such as diagnostics or partial results. A domain outcome answers “what happened in the modeled world?” and may represent denial or cancellation even when the computation behaved perfectly. Keeping those meanings apart prevents a business event from being mistaken for a bug, or an implementation failure from becoming a permanent domain variant.

title: 9  Doctrine: Principles, Decision Guides, and Named Anti-Patterns
text:
9.2 Decision guides
The principles explain the defaults; the guides turn them into ordered questions for a concrete design review.
Formulated as the questions to ask, in order, rather than flowcharts to follow mechanically.
Which object system? Is it fundamentally a homogeneous vector that must slice and live in data frames? — vctrs. Does it have identity and a lifetime, with observers sharing its changes? — R6 or an environment. Is it a domain value with laws and dispatchable behavior? — S7. Is it a veneer for ecosystem politeness? — S3. Mixed answers mean a hybrid, which is normal.
Which lifecycle policy? Is ordinary revision through replacement part of the concept? — editable value. Is it a completed fact whose public API should forbid revision? — read-only snapshot. Must aliases observe the same evolving resource or process? — reference owner. A value holding a reference is a hybrid, not a deeply isolated value.
Which sum-type encoding? Do variants differ in fields, or does behavior dispatch on them? — subclass family under an abstract parent. Do they differ only in the tag? — enum-valued property. Is it several primitive shapes or domain classes lawful in one slot? — union. Is the wire genuinely one bag with conditional fields, variants are many and trivial, and dispatch is never needed? — a discriminator plus class validator, chosen consciously as denormalization.
Which semantic-type tier? Does the concept merely repeat a validation shape across sites? — a reused property definition. Must it be impossible to confuse with its base primitive, or does dispatch need it, while it remains truly a primitive? — a class inheriting the base type. Does it have parts, or operations of its own? — a composite class.
Stored field, identity, or boundary-normalized? Can two instances of the class differ on it? If no — identity (computed property or serializer-injected). If yes — must round-trips preserve the caller’s exact value? If yes — stored, with lenient parsing at the boundary and one canonical stored form. Might the spec extend the value set? — stored enum with a parse-time version gate.
Where does a rule belong? Does it mention one property’s intrinsic shape or value? — property contract. Several properties of one object? — class validator. References among contained objects? — aggregate root. External data, metadata, resources, or authority? — contextual operation.
Condition, computational result, or domain outcome? Is the event a contract violation that should unwind control flow? — condition. Is expected failure composed with a computation? — result value plus an explicit short-circuit or accumulation protocol. Is the event meaningful in the domain regardless of computation mechanics? — domain outcome family. Design adapters among channels at named boundaries.
Faithful conversion, adapter, compiler, or intermediate representation? Does the target preserve the same meaning pairwise? — S7::convert(). Is the translation lossy, contextual, one-to-many, policy-bearing, or diagnostic? — a named adapter or compiler. Have multiple real inputs or outputs exposed a stable shared semantics? — consider an intermediate representation then, not before.
How deep should an embedded language go? Does anything analyze or transform the expressions, or target more than one output format? If no — opaque passthrough, with the engine’s validator as judge. Do humans hand-write the expressions painfully? — constructor combinators (shallow embedding). Is analysis, optimization, or multi-target translation the product? — typed AST with generic passes (deep embedding). Representation as deep as the analysis, and no deeper.

title: 9  Doctrine: Principles, Decision Guides, and Named Anti-Patterns
text:
9.3 Anti-pattern catalog
The guides identify a choice before implementation. The names below identify the recurring failure shapes once code or a design proposal exists.
Named, so design reviews can point at them.
Schema cosplay. Mirroring incidental foreign structure as nominal domain meaning without identifying the consumers or guarantees it serves. A generated transport facade can be legitimate when flatness or exact fields are authoritative; field count alone proves nothing. Tell: every foreign interface becomes a hand-maintained class, yet downstream code still interprets raw tags and nullable combinations.
Validator soup. The same law independently defined in the constructor, property validator, class validator, and boundary schema. One authoritative declaration may have several deliberate enforcements or projections; the failure is duplicated authority with no agreement tests. Tell: fixing one rule requires unrelated edits in several places.
Shotgun parsing. Input checks interleaved with processing across many functions, no single point after which input is known-good, rejection possible after side effects. Tell: is.null() and is.character() guards deep in core logic; functions that “defensively” re-check their own package’s objects.
Boolean blindness. Check functions returning TRUE/FALSE whose callers immediately need the why or the what — so they re-derive it. Tell: if (is_valid(x)) { ... } followed by code that re-inspects x for the very facts validity established. Return parsed evidence, not verdicts.
The God validator. One class validator enforcing property-local rules, cross-property rules, and collection rules in a hundred lines. Placement discipline lost; every rung’s law in one place, none assumable by the others. Tell: a class validator that re-checks types.
Convert-everything. Routing lossy, contextual, one-to-many translation through a coercion generic because it exists. Coercion generics (S7::convert(from, to)) suit faithful pairwise conversion; translation with diagnostics, options, and asset generation deserves named functions with room for a context argument and a report. Tell: a convert method with side effects or a dozen options.
Expression-system envy. Re-implementing an engine’s expression type system in property validators — badly, partially, and forever chasing the spec. The engine’s validator owns rung 0. Tell: a validator that walks nested lists interpreting operator names.
Decorative hierarchy. Inheritance introduced to share field names or to “organize” classes that never dispatch differently. Dispatch will eventually take the fake is-a seriously. Tell: an abstract parent with one child, or parents whose children never appear in a method signature.
The accidental reference owner. Domain facts held in R6 “for convenience,” creating shared identity where observers did not need it. Tell: $clone() calls sprinkled defensively and lifecycle tests for what consumers treat as a value.
Nullable confusion. NULL doing triple duty as “required but not yet supplied,” “explicitly cleared,” and “omitted on the wire,” with no presence policy. Tell: code that cannot distinguish an untouched field from a cleared one; serializers with ad-hoc per-field if (!is.null()) decisions.
Premature DSL. Combinators, quotation, and clever printing built before any user wrote the target structures by hand long enough to reveal which constructions are actually painful. The DSL then ossifies the wrong abstractions. Tell: a DSL whose vocabulary mirrors the wire format one-to-one instead of the domain’s own idioms.
Effectful getter. A property that reads a file, calls an API, or mutates a cache. Data access becomes action at a distance; cost and effects become invisible at every @. Tell: property access inside a loop dominating a profile; getters needing error handling.
Boundary leakage. Wire names, omit-empty decisions, or dialect quirks appearing in core logic instead of the one serializer pair. Tell: "source-layer" (the wire spelling) as a string anywhere except to_wire()/from_wire().

title: 9  Doctrine: Principles, Decision Guides, and Named Anti-Patterns
text:
9.4 A closing note on judgment
The principles compress experience, but they trade against each other in real designs: parse-don’t-validate argues for strictness at the boundary while round-trip fidelity argues for permissive pass-through nodes; earned abstraction argues for waiting while semantic atoms argue for naming meanings early; shallow hierarchies argue against intermediate classes while shared schema sometimes argues for them. The earlier documents exist so that when two principles collide, the reasons behind each are available and the trade can be made explicitly, on the record, instead of by whichever slogan was remembered first.

title: 10  Playbooks: One Workflow, Different Pressures
text:
10.1 The shared opening workflow
These situations differ, but they should not begin from different design philosophies. Each starts with the same workflow and then emphasizes the steps where its pressures are unusual.
Choose a playbook by asking two questions: where does the truth about correctness live, and what kind of life does the artifact have? A published format points to external conformance; foreign type definitions to translation; an invented vocabulary to language design; deferred expensive work to configuration; a live resource to fact/process separation; and third-party implementations to an extension contract. A real package often needs several answers. The workflow below stays shared so those parts can meet without inventing incompatible design philosophies.
Use these eight moves for every S7 design.

title: 10  Playbooks: One Workflow, Different Pressures
text:
10.1.1 1. Inventory meanings and consumers
Name the concepts the program cares about and the consumers that need them: constructors, operations, serializers, databases, interfaces, workers, or external validators. Record what each consumer currently infers or re-checks.


10.1.2 2. Sketch representative values and variants
Draw a small top-down slice before building foundations. Include an ordinary case, an edge case, and an unknown or extension case. Distinguish containment from references and value facts from live owners.


10.1.3 3. Inventory property contracts
For every property, record shape, cardinality, membership, bounds, caller-requiredness, stored presence, nullability, emptiness, default ownership, and wire omission. Decide whether meaning belongs to a reusable property or must travel as a semantic class.


10.1.4 4. Place rules at the smallest informed boundary
Put intrinsic rules on properties, relationships among one object’s fields on the class, cross-object rules on an aggregate root, and data-, host-, or authority-dependent rules in a named contextual operation. Do not ask a boundary to certify facts it cannot see.


10.1.5 5. Co-design operations and failure policy
List domain verbs, accepted concepts, result meanings, and laws. Decide where generic dispatch clarifies variation. State which failures are conditions, which are outcome values, and whether outcomes short-circuit or accumulate.


10.1.6 6. Extract only repeated recipes
After the representative slice works, extract repeated property factories, validators, or projection metadata. Important meanings may be named immediately; generalized machinery should earn its cost through repetition or multiple consumers.


10.1.7 7. Define transformations and projections
Name supported edits, parsers, serializers, renderers, schema projections, and host-binding steps. For each, state what is preserved, normalized, rejected, or lost. Reserve S7::convert() for faithful representation changes; name policy-bearing work parse_*(), adapt_*(), or compile_*().


10.1.8 8. Write acceptance laws
Test promised behavior and downstream simplification:

construction followed by supported replacement remains intrinsically valid;
preparing a run resolves every contextual bound before execution;
serialize then parse preserves a named equality relation;
render then reflect is semantically equal within documented dialect limits;
every known variant has methods for required operations;
consumers no longer repeat scalar, range, presence, or reference checks.

title: 10  Playbooks: One Workflow, Different Pressures
text:
10.2 Playbook 1: Modeling an existing specification
Pressure. Contract authority is external, versions change, and unknown content may matter.
Opening. You have a published format—perhaps STAC, GeoJSON, OpenAPI, or a style document—and users must construct, edit, and emit conforming documents. Collect the specification, machine-readable schema, official validator, reference implementation, and representative public examples before choosing classes. The first design artifact is a small vertical slice, not a transcription of every schema definition.

Include the specification, official validator, reference implementation, and representative documents in the consumer inventory.
Sketch a vertical slice rather than transcribing the schema: one typed node, one open node, one reference edge, and one round trip.
Record presence separately from nullability and defaults. External formats commonly distinguish omitted, null, empty, and defaulted values.
Put document-wide references and uniqueness at the aggregate root; retain the external validator as conformance oracle.
Design operations users need inside R. Those operations, not schema field count, determine which nodes deserve semantic classes.
Extract recipes from recurring shapes or an owned machine-readable specification. Generated native classes are legitimate when source and authority are explicit.
State the unknown-key and version policy per node. Preserve extensions only if serializers and transformations can keep them.
Test conformance and the named round-trip relation. Byte identity, canonical equality, and domain equality are different laws.

stacbuildr shows native constructors plus external conformance. S7schema shows detailed entries remaining under external-schema authority.

10.2.1 A parser/serializer slice
The slice below keeps wire spelling at the boundary, injects the constant type field at serialization, remembers whether an engine default was actually supplied, and preserves unknown keys. That presence bit is necessary: without it, parsing an explicit minzoom = 0 and parsing an omitted minzoom would collapse two wire states that a later specification version may treat differently.
to_wire <- S7::new_generic("to_wire", "x")

vector_source <- S7::new_class(
  "vector_source",
  properties = list(
    url = S7::class_character,
    min_zoom = S7::new_property(S7::class_numeric, default = 0),
    min_zoom_supplied = S7::new_property(S7::class_logical, default = FALSE),
    extensions = S7::new_property(S7::class_list, default = list())
  )
)

source_from_wire <- function(x) {
  if (!is.list(x) || is.null(x[["url"]])) {
    cli::cli_abort("A vector source must contain {.field url}.")
  }

  known <- c("type", "url", "minzoom")
  supplied <- "minzoom" %in% names(x)

  vector_source(
    url = x[["url"]],
    min_zoom = if (supplied) x[["minzoom"]] else 0,
    min_zoom_supplied = supplied,
    extensions = x[setdiff(names(x), known)]
  )
}

S7::method(to_wire, vector_source) <- function(x) {
  out <- c(list(type = "vector", url = x@url), x@extensions)
  if (x@min_zoom_supplied) {
    out[["minzoom"]] <- x@min_zoom
  }
  out
}
The law is not byte identity: key order may change. It is equality of known meaning plus preservation of untouched extensions and suppliedness. The short trap is normalizing before recording evidence. Its consequence is a serializer that cannot distinguish an omitted default from an explicit value, so an apparently harmless round trip silently rewrites user intent.

title: 10  Playbooks: One Workflow, Different Pressures
text:
10.3 Playbook 2: Translating foreign type definitions
Pressure. A foreign type system expresses distinctions R may encode differently.
Opening. The source of truth is a TypeScript declaration, Rust enum, Go struct, C header, or protobuf schema. This is not yet a domain model. Begin with a ledger that records what crosses the boundary and what is lost, then separate generated transport shapes from hand-designed semantic concepts. Direction determines ownership. If R only decodes a foreign artifact, the foreign validator and parser own conformance while the R model may be a one-way semantic projection. If R also emits artifacts, the encoder owns omission, defaults, and unknown-field preservation, and conformance must be tested in that direction as well. A bidirectional claim therefore requires two boundary contracts, not one vaguely “equivalent” class graph.

Inventory foreign meanings and both sides’ consumers.
Sketch tagged unions, newtypes, optional fields, and extension records.
Create a translation ledger for required, absent, null, defaulted, and unknown values. Do not collapse undefined, explicit null, and an absent key without policy.
Separate transport checks from domain invariants and host-context rules.
Import behavioral laws, not only shapes. Ownership, read-only declarations, or capabilities may need operations rather than properties.
Extract translation recipes only after a construct recurs.
Name direction and loss: decoding, encoding, adapting, or compiling are not automatically faithful conversions.
Test conformance in each direction and use a named equality relation for bidirectional claims.

A tagged union may become concrete variants under an abstract dispatch parent, but the parent is not sealed and does not prove coverage. Maintain method-coverage tests when a known family must be handled.
The trap is shape-only translation. It produces classes that resemble the foreign declarations while dropping ownership, equality, readonly, and presence laws. The consequence appears later as incompatible round trips and defensive checks spread across every consumer.

text:
10.5 Playbook 4: Configuring expensive computation
Pressure. Some mistakes are cheap during setup but expensive during execution; other rules need data not yet available.
Opening. A configuration exists now, but the data, host, or compute budget needed to finish checking it arrives later. Split specification from preparation: construction records intrinsic intent; prepare() resolves context; execution accepts only the prepared certificate.

Inventory decisions and setup, preparation, execution, reporting, and interface consumers.
Sketch RunSpecification, candidate values, and PreparedRun rather than one undifferentiated bag.
Record bounded scalars, enums, optional selections, vector values, candidate sets, and default ownership.
Keep intrinsic and cross-property rules in the specification; resolve data dimensions or host resources in prepare().
Make execute() accept the prepared value so it does not repeat contextual checks. Define failure before expensive work.
Extract property specifications only when repeated declarations or several projections justify them.
Define supported edits and projections to schemas, documentation, or interfaces.
Test that preparation resolves deferred rules and execution contains no duplicate range or candidate-intent inference.

rtemis is the focused public exhibit for candidate intent, contextual bounds, and multiple projections.
Inspection is part of the contract, not print-method decoration. For each setting, expose both value and state:

supplied — the caller chose the value;
defaulted — R or the external authority supplied it under a named policy;
resolved — preparation checked or derived it against actual context;
pending — a declared contextual rule still lacks the inputs needed to decide it.

A printed RunSpecification should make pending checks visible; a PreparedRun should contain none. The trap is late rediscovery: execution re-infers whether a value was intentional and discovers a data-bound violation after expensive setup. The consequence is both wasted compute and a result that cannot explain which decisions were actually made.

title: 10  Playbooks: One Workflow, Different Pressures
section: 10.6 Playbook 5: Binding portable definitions to live authority
text:
10.6 Playbook 5: Binding portable definitions to live authority
Pressure. A valid request is not authorization, and a live process has identity that a portable value does not.
Opening. The system contains both portable descriptions and something with a lifetime: a session, connection, device, browser, conversation, or worker. Sort every noun into fact or process before choosing its object system. Then place the authority boundary between the portable request and the live owner.

Inventory definitions, host policy, executable capabilities, owners, and completed outcomes.
Sketch TaskDefinition, AuthorizedTask, a live runner, and TaskOutcome as distinct concepts.
Put identifiers, resource requests, and symbolic capability names in portable values—not connections, closures, or secrets.
Validate requested relationships locally; bind capabilities and enforce authority ceilings in a host-context operation.
Decide which operational failures throw and which become named outcomes.
Extract permission and resource recipes after concrete tasks reveal repetition.
Define serialization before binding and projections of runtime state to inspectable values.
Test that serialization contains no executable resources, unauthorized requests fail before effects, and outcomes require no flag interpretation.

deputy illustrates tools, permissions, limits, and a live agent run.
The lifecycle argument is causal. Aliases must observe one connection or in-progress stream, so that process needs reference identity. Completed requests, turns, settings, and outcomes no longer evolve, so they become S7 values that can be compared, serialized, and tested without the resource. The owner should therefore stay thin: lifecycle and orchestration around value-in/value-out operations. If a value carries a reference payload, state that explicitly because replacement and outer validation do not observe mutation inside the payload.
The trap is turning facts into owners for convenience. Its consequence is defensive cloning, shared-state test setup, and uncertainty about whether two callers are looking at the same evolving thing or two equal facts.

title: 10  Playbooks: One Workflow, Different Pressures
text:
10.7 Playbook 6: Designing an extension surface
Pressure. Third parties implement operations, so signatures alone are insufficient.
Opening. Other packages will implement your storage backend, provider, renderer, or engine. Draft verbs and laws before polishing the abstract class. The class gives dispatch a place to stand; the real product is a stable generic set, behavioral laws, capability protocol, and executable conformance suite.

Inventory implementors and framework consumers.
Sketch at least two implementations, including a small test implementation.
Keep implementor-specific state out of the parent unless all implementations share its meaning.
Put framework-checkable preconditions at the framework boundary and implementation-specific context inside methods.
Define required generics, optional capabilities, results, failure policy, and laws before freezing hierarchies.
Extract helpers after two implementations reveal common structure.
Define compatibility and adaptation rules for contract evolution.
Export a conformance suite that exercises laws, capabilities, and missing-method diagnostics.

An abstract parent gives dispatch a place to stand. It does not seal the family, prove every method exists, or replace a conformance suite.
The second implementation is not ceremonial. Build one realistic implementation and one deliberately small in-memory implementation before freezing signatures. The second exposes assumptions that accidentally belong to the first—filesystem paths in a generic, provider-specific state on the root, or a law that only one backend can satisfy. Run both through the same conformance function, including method-coverage and missing-capability cases.
The trap is a one-implementation interface. Its consequence is an API that looks extensible but requires the second implementor either to emulate the first backend’s accidents or to bypass the advertised contract.

title: 10  Playbooks: One Workflow, Different Pressures
text:
10.8 Combining playbooks
Composition means assigning each concern its own authority and lifecycle, not blending the checklists. In a map-style package, the document follows the specification playbook, embedded expressions begin at the language playbook’s opaque rung, and build options use the configuration playbook. The style itself remains a value; no live-resource playbook is needed unless a renderer session or remote engine actually introduces shared identity.
An API client combines them differently. Authentication, retries, and rate limits belong to a thin live owner; typed request and response payloads follow the foreign-types or published-specification playbook; multiple provider backends invoke the extension-surface playbook and its conformance suite. The shared eight-step workflow keeps the joins explicit: each part names its consumers, rule horizon, failure channel, transformation boundary, and laws.
This matters because the playbooks intentionally disagree about first artifacts. A specification needs a gold-file slice, a translation needs a ledger, a language needs hand-written targets, configuration needs visible pending state, a live resource needs a fact/process cut, and an extension surface needs a second implementation. Combining them preserves those differences while giving the package one design vocabulary.

title: 10  Playbooks: One Workflow, Different Pressures
text:
10.9 Choosing a playbook
The doctrine decision guides are the canonical compact reference for choosing representations, lifecycles, failure channels, conversion boundaries, and embedded-language depth. Return here once that decision identifies the kind of design work to perform; the playbooks above supply the corresponding sequence and verification steps.

11.1 The position
Opening principles become useful only when plausible designs are compared against actual consumers. This chapter follows one semantic-document problem through three defensible representations:
None is the inevitable S7 answer. Streaming does not force a particular owner architecture, a large field count does not disqualify native classes, and metamodel size alone does not justify a schema engine. The choice turns on guarantees and operations.
Suppose a package works with style documents containing named sources, typed layers, paint settings, references from layers to sources, and embedded expressions. It must support:
Before choosing classes, apply the shared opening workflow.

text:
11.5 Comparing candidates by consumer

11.5.1 Construction
A property-rich model gives the strongest discoverable constructor surface. The hybrid gives strong constructors for known concepts and an extension escape hatch. The open bag minimizes translation but depends more heavily on boundary validation and documentation.


11.5.2 Supported transformation
For add_layer(), all three can enforce root-level id and reference laws if the operation goes through a validated root. The difference is bypass risk: native replacement paths can revalidate declared contracts, while ordinary list mutation requires convention or an explicit validation pass.


11.5.3 External evolution
The property-rich model can evolve safely when generation and versioning are disciplined. The hybrid absorbs unknown additions but must preserve and merge them. The open bag accepts change most easily but exposes fewer guarantees.


11.5.4 Projection and interface generation
Property-rich declarations help when documentation, schema, and UI consumers need the same metadata. A hybrid can project the typed portion and label extensions separately. An open bag should project from its external schema rather than infer contracts from observed values.


11.5.5 Analysis and dispatch
If legend generation, field usage, or renderer behavior varies by layer kind, typed variants earn their cost. If serialization is the only consumer, open data plus validation may suffice.

title: 11  The Middlegame: Choosing Representation Under Pressure
11  The Middlegame: Choosing Representation Under Pressure
text:
11.7 Conversion pressure: three different jobs

11.7.1 Faithful conversion
Use S7::convert() when two representations preserve the same meaning without policy, diagnostics, or contextual choices. The acceptance law should be a genuine inverse or clearly named equivalence.


11.7.2 Adapter or compiler
Use parse_style(), adapt_style(), or compile_style() when work is tolerant, lossy, contextual, one-to-many, version-aware, or diagnostic-producing. A parser may preserve unknown variants that a compiler later rejects. Naming policy is more honest than calling this conversion.


11.7.3 Earned intermediate representation
Do not create a universal style IR by unioning every foreign field. Earn an IR when at least two real inputs or outputs reveal stable shared semantics and operations consume those semantics. sqlr earns its middle representation through rendering, reflection, semantic comparison, and diffing. One serializer does not provide the same evidence.

title: 11  The Middlegame: Choosing Representation Under Pressure
11  The Middlegame: Choosing Representation Under Pressure
text:
11.9 What remains unsettled
This comparison does not decide how large property metadata should become, when an id deserves promotion from shared property to class, whether expression analysis will justify typed nodes, how version migration should work, or which equality relation users need. Those remain in the open-questions ledger.

title: 11  The Middlegame: Choosing Representation Under Pressure
text:
11.10 Keeping the decision live
Record consequential choices in a five-field decision journal:

Decision — the representation or boundary being chosen.
Pressure — the concrete consumer, law, or cost forcing attention.
Options — the plausible candidates considered.
Choice — the selected option and its accepted concessions.
Doctrine — the principle followed or overruled, with the reason.

For this scenario, the entry would say that layer variants remain typed while unknown fields use extension bags; the pressure is native edit operations plus foreign round-trip fidelity; the alternatives are the three candidates above; the concession is split authority; and the doctrine trade is honest alternatives balanced against external-schema authority.
Review the journal at complexity checkpoints, not by calendar: the first mutator tests invariant placement; the first parser/serializer pair tests presence and equality together; the second output target tests whether an intermediate representation is emerging; the tenth repeated declaration tests whether generation now amortizes; and the first external implementation tests whether generics plus laws form a real contract. A checkpoint may move the design toward any candidate. The balanced conclusion remains: complexity and field count are pressures to price, not automatic votes for or against native classes.

title: Appendix A — Open Questions: The Inquiry Ledger
text:
A.1 Scale of property metadata
This ledger records what the design guidance does not yet settle: hypotheses resting on sparse evidence, version-sensitive mechanics, and tensions for which either choice can fail. Its purpose is movement, not accumulation. Questions graduate into doctrine when public documentation, source, tests, or reproducible released-version probes support a bounded recommendation. They retreat when counterexamples expose a missing condition, and the affected doctrine should then be amended rather than silently defended.
Every entry should preserve the competing risks. More metadata can align projections but make authoring and startup expensive. A richer semantic model can enable analysis but duplicate a foreign authority. Strict admission can protect invariants but destroy unknown content needed for round trips. The ledger is useful only if it asks what evidence distinguishes those losses, not merely whether a favored technique can be made to work.
rtemis shows contract-as-data driving validation, defaults, schema output, interfaces, and contextual preparation. The unresolved question is when that machinery pays for itself.
Evidence needed: maintenance histories comparing handwritten and metadata-driven properties; contributor cost for adding or debugging a property; alignment tests across releases; and examples where such a system was simplified or removed.

title: Appendix A — Open Questions: The Inquiry Ledger
section: A.2 Promotion from reusable property to semantic class
text:
A.2 Promotion from reusable property to semantic class
A shared property names a contract cheaply; a class lets the value travel independently and participate in dispatch. The boundary remains judgment-dependent when a concept is meaningful but has no operation of its own.
Evidence needed: cases where early promotion prevented ambiguity or rework; cases where it only added wrapping overhead; and criteria based on extraction, independent persistence, or operation vocabulary.

title: Appendix A — Open Questions: The Inquiry Ledger
section: A.3 Direct adaptation versus semantic IR
text:
A.3 Direct adaptation versus semantic IR
A pairwise adapter is simpler for one source and target. An IR may reduce duplication across several sources and targets, but an “uber-schema” can merely accumulate incidental fields.
Evidence needed: multiple real inputs or outputs sharing stable semantics; operations that consume shared meaning independently of serialization; preservation and loss matrices; and migration experience showing whether an IR reduces or relocates complexity.
The competing risks are premature generalization and adapter proliferation. An IR introduced before stable shared meaning is visible becomes another schema to migrate. Waiting too long leaves every pairwise adapter to rediscover normalization, equality, and loss policy. Graduation therefore requires evidence from independent consumers, not the size of the class graph.

title: Appendix A — Open Questions: The Inquiry Ledger
text:
A.4 Typed expression catalogs
Opaque expressions preserve engine authority and version flexibility. Typed nodes enable analysis, safer construction, and multi-target compilation. The point at which analysis justifies the catalog remains domain-specific.
Evidence needed: a substantive consumer beyond serialization; measured versioning cost; a policy for unknown operators; and evidence that combinators are insufficient but a full AST is maintainable.

title: Appendix A — Open Questions: The Inquiry Ledger
section: A.5 Deep value semantics with references
text:
A.5 Deep value semantics with references
An S7 value may contain an environment, R6 object, external pointer, connection, or cache. Replacing the outer value does not make referenced internals independent, and inner mutation does not automatically re-run outer validation.
Open questions include which payloads should be forbidden, snapshotted, or excluded from equality and serialization; whether external memo tables keyed by semantic content are reliable; and how APIs should state shallow versus deep guarantees.

title: Appendix A — Open Questions: The Inquiry Ledger
section: A.6 Method coverage for open families
text:
A.6 Method coverage for open families
Abstract parents and fallback methods do not seal a family. Registries and tests can check known variants, but extensions may add classes after those checks run.
Open questions: whether coverage belongs at test time, registration, or first use; how optional generics differ from missing methods; and how third parties run reusable conformance suites. Native sealed-family or exhaustiveness support would change the guidance.

title: Appendix A — Open Questions: The Inquiry Ledger
section: A.7 Explicit null, omission, and defaults
text:
A.7 Explicit null, omission, and defaults
R’s NULL, absent arguments, empty vectors, NA, and absent wire keys can represent different states. Preserving every needed distinction remains difficult, especially for generated constructors.
Evidence needed: released-version probes for omitted arguments versus explicit NULL; public formats where omission changes behavior; ergonomic constructor patterns; and serializer laws for omitted, null, empty, and defaulted states.

title: Appendix A — Open Questions: The Inquiry Ledger
text:
A.8 Survival of unknown extensions
A pass-through bag promises fidelity only if every supported transformation and serialization cycle preserves it. Typed and raw state can collide when a specification promotes a formerly unknown field.
Open questions: whether extensions survive repeated read-modify-write cycles; how upgrades detect collisions; whether preservation is byte-level, structural, or normalized; and whether untrusted extensions create security or resource risks. Corpus-based round-trip tests across released format versions are needed.

title: Appendix A — Open Questions: The Inquiry Ledger
text:
A.9 Persistence and class evolution
Persisted S7 values may outlive the package version that created them. Current guidance prefers durable wire representations parsed by current code, but compatibility policy is under-specified.
Open questions: explicit schema versions; migration registration and composition; cross-release compatibility promises; serialized validator environments; and S7 mechanics for revalidation after loading. Version-pinned cross-release probes and public persistence policies are needed. RDS compatibility should be stated narrowly rather than assumed.

title: Appendix A — Open Questions: The Inquiry Ledger
text:
A.10 Equality relations
Exact identical() representation, canonical equality, domain equality, and observational equivalence answer different questions. Packages often need several, especially for reflected or normalized documents.
Open questions: which relation powers user comparison; whether canonicalization is stored or computed; how extensions participate; and how diagnostics suppress incidental noise. sqlr supplies one model; recurrence elsewhere would clarify reusable patterns.

title: Appendix A — Open Questions: The Inquiry Ledger
section: A.11 Strict parsing and tolerant admission
text:
A.11 Strict parsing and tolerant admission
Strict known construction can coexist with a tolerant parser preserving unknown or partial variants plus diagnostics. The unresolved issue is when tolerance becomes unsafe or misleading.
Evidence needed: security boundaries requiring rejection; tools that preserve partial documents but refuse compilation; policies for diagnostics and revalidation; and issue histories showing whether partial values clarify or defer failures.

title: Appendix A — Open Questions: The Inquiry Ledger
text:
A.12 Aggregate-root granularity
Deep documents resist a simple “one document, one validator” rule. A single root can enforce cross-reference invariants in one place, but it also makes a small edit pay for traversal of an entire graph and can turn unrelated subtrees into one consistency boundary. Nested roots localize construction, replacement, and diagnostics, but delegation can miss invariants that cross their boundaries or duplicate checks at several levels.
Evidence needed: real document models with cross-references at multiple depths; mutation traces showing which edits require global knowledge; failure reports comparing one root with delegated roots; and examples where aggregate boundaries remained stable as the format evolved. The question should graduate only as a decision rule for choosing a boundary, not as a fixed maximum tree depth.

title: Appendix A — Open Questions: The Inquiry Ledger
text:
A.13 Diagnostic duplication threshold
The guidance permits a cheap, documented duplicate check when it catches a bad input at a boundary with a materially better message. “Cheap” remains undefined. One duplicate can improve locality; several can drift, disagree on edge cases, and obscure which rule is authoritative.
Evidence needed: maintenance histories where duplicate checks did or did not drift; tests that prove equivalence to the authoritative rule; measurements for checks on realistic payloads; and user evidence that the earlier diagnostic changes recovery. A candidate threshold is that a duplicate must have one named authority, an explicit equivalence test, negligible cost on the boundary’s expected payload, and no independent evolution. A duplicate that needs its own exceptions or release policy has become a second authority and should retreat.

title: Appendix A — Open Questions: The Inquiry Ledger
Appendix A — Open Questions: The Inquiry Ledger
text:
A.15 Focused benchmark agenda
The useful question is not whether S7 is “fast.” Measurements should compare design alternatives at the points where the guidance makes a choice, with R and S7 versions, payload shape, garbage-collection policy, and warm-up stated.
Bulk construction. Compare constructor-per-node construction with documented deferred-validation or batching mechanisms across realistic flat and nested values. Record allocations and validation work as well as elapsed time; a fast path that weakens the certification boundary is not equivalent.
Grouped versus sequential replacement. Compare S7::set_props() with sequential @<- updates for several property counts and validator costs. Measure intermediate copies and validator invocations, and include a case where only the final grouped state is valid.
Nested copy cost. Vary top-level width, nesting depth, and shared payload size to determine what replacement copies and what remains shared. Include two-binding divergence checks so an optimization is not mistaken for a semantic change.
Hot-loop dispatch. Compare direct calls, S3 dispatch, and S7 single and multiple dispatch in representative compiler or tree-walk loops. Report the fraction of total pass time attributable to dispatch; isolated nanoseconds do not establish architectural significance.
Metamodel startup. Measure package load and class-definition cost as the number and richness of property factories increase, including declaration validation and generated projections. This tests the author-safety benefit against interactive and worker-startup latency.
Serialized-corpus overhead. Compare many small S7 objects, aggregate serialization, and durable wire forms across corpus sizes. Separate payload bytes from repeated class or validator metadata, and test cross-version load behavior rather than treating successful deserialization as compatibility.
These benchmarks should graduate guidance only when they reproduce across released versions and realistic graphs. Surprising results should first narrow the recommendation; they should not become a universal performance claim.

title: Appendix A — Open Questions: The Inquiry Ledger
text:
A.16 Evidence tripwires
Revise the guidance if S7 adds sealed classes, exhaustiveness checks, or load-time migration; several packages sustain generated native graphs from owned semantic specifications; property metadata is removed as uneconomic; a typed AST is collapsed; an open bag beats a semantic model on long-term correctness; or public round-trip corpora reveal systematic extension loss.
The ledger should also collect counterexamples: designs that violate current defaults and work well, migrations away from S7 with stated reasons, and duplicated checks that remain aligned because their diagnostic value is worth the cost.
A counterexample entry should name the pressure the current guidance missed, the competing risk that dominated, and the smallest exception that explains the result. Repeated retreats are evidence that the doctrine’s boundary is wrong; an isolated exception is not permission to erase the boundary.

title: Appendix B — Glossary
text:
Terms in this glossary name recurring design distinctions rather than new S7 APIs. Each definition links to its principal treatment in the book.

Aggregate root

The object boundary that sees a complete consistency unit and can enforce relationships among its contained values. See the checking ladder.

Canonical equality

Equality after applying documented normalization rules, without requiring exact R representation identity. See identity and equality.

Contextual preparation

A named operation that combines an intrinsically valid value with external data, metadata, resources, or authority and returns a value recording what was resolved. See contextual preparation.

Domain equality

Equality defined by meaning in the problem domain rather than exact storage representation. See round-trip equivalence.

Invariant

A condition that must remain true for a value or consistency boundary throughout its supported lifecycle. See retained knowledge.

Operation contract

The meaning, accepted concepts, result, failure policy, and laws shared by every implementation of an operation. See defining operations.

Property contract

The class, shape, cardinality, presence policy, default behavior, and intrinsic constraints attached to one property position. See the property inventory.

Projection

A deliberate representation derived from an authoritative model, such as a schema, serializer output, interface description, or documentation page. See schema architectures.

Reference owner

An object with shared identity or a live lifecycle whose aliases must observe the same evolving state. See the lifecycle policies.

Semantic class

A nominal class that preserves a domain concept independently so it can travel through the program or participate in dispatch. See the semantic carriers.

Snapshot

A value representing a fact at a point in time, often with a public policy that forbids revision. See the lifecycle policies.

Sum type

A representation of alternatives in which a value is exactly one of several meaningful variants. See alternatives and variants.

Wire representation

The serialized form exchanged with another system, distinct from the program’s semantic domain model. See documents and schemas.

C.7 Evidence labels

Official mechanism: documented by S7 or another authoritative public specification.
Public source observation: visible in a linked public repository; behavior may change. Version-sensitive observations should use an immutable revision link.
Public test assertion: encoded in a linked package test suite.
Released-version probe: reproducible execution naming R, S7, and package versions.
Editorial proposal: guidance offered for evaluation, not a claim that a package implements it.

A source comment, README statement, or single implementation can motivate a question. It should not become a universal claim without corroborating evidence.
